articles.title: Prosecution flags 'floating' P41.7-M manager's check linked to Rodrigo, Sara Duterte
articles.summary: The House prosecution panel on Wednesday flagged a P41.7-million worth of manager"s check linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte and Vice President Sara Duterte that was supposedly “floating” for…

blocks.text: The House prosecution panel on Wednesday flagged a P41.7-million worth of manager’s check linked to former president Rodrigo Duterte and Vice President Sara Duterte that was supposedly “floating” for years and was not being reflected in year-end balances.

On Day 35 of the impeachment trial, Marwin Galvez, division head for Central Manila branches of Bank of the Philippine Islands (BPI), confirmed the existence of a joint peso time deposit opened on January 22, 2010, in the bank’s Julia Vargas Branch under the name “Rodrigo Roa Duterte or Rodrigo Roa Duterte and Sara Z. Duterte.”
During his direct examination by private prosecutor James Bryan Alih, Galvez said the time deposit had a principal amount of P40,650,000.
Galvez said that the time deposit had 12 rollover periods or renewals. At the last renewal in February 2011, he said the amount already increased to P41.7 million, including the interest.

“If a time deposit certificate matures and is no longer renewed, the proceeds of the matured time deposit are credited to the settlement account,” Galvez said, affirming that the settlement account is the Julia Vargas Branch.
In March 2011, the BPI official said a credit and debit memo showed that a manager’s check was purchased for P41.7 million.
Galvez noted that a manager’s check has a period of validity of only six months.
Seven months after the purchase of the manager’s check, or in October 2011, Alih pointed out that another credit and debit memo reflected that a manager's check with the same amount was unutilized.

“When you say unutilized, Your Honor, ibig sabihin hindi po siya nagamit, depende sa sitwasyon. ‘Pag lumagpas ng six months nang hindi nagagamit ‘yung payee, kung kanino nakapangalan ang manager’s check, nasa desisyon ng payee kung nasa kanya na ang position ng manager’s check,” Galvez explained.

(When you say ‘unutilized,’ Your Honor, it means it wasn’t used, depending on the situation. If six months pass without the manager’s check being used, it is up to the payee or the person named on the check to decide what to do with it.)

“Puwede po ang kliyente, kung saan galing ang pondo na pinambili ng manager’s check, kung hindi na niya gagamitin ang manager’s check, puwede niyang i-request na ibalik po ito sa pinanggalingan ng account,” he added.
(The client, the one whose funds were used to purchase the manager’s check, can also request that the amount be returned to the source account if they no longer intend to use the check.)
Defense counsel Michael Poa objected to the presentation of evidence on the ground of relevance.
Alih said that the prosecution intends to prove a "pattern," that a transaction in 2011 moved around for several more years and was later on used to purchase insurance policies.

“We will attempt to show, Your Honor, that later, this amount—this P41 million, tapos meron pa pong (and an additional) P55 million, at some point, we will try to prove, magsasama sila ulit sa (they will be combined in the) Julia Vargas Branch, and they will use this to purchase several insurance policies for the same amount,” the private prosecutor said.

“Ang punto lang naman po eventually is that ‘yung manager’s check na pinapaikot, hindi nakikita sa year-end balance kasi naka-float ‘yung pera na ‘yun. ‘Yun lang naman ‘yung gusto naming i-establish as a baseline,” he added.
(The only point is that the manager's check that is being circulated is not reflected in the year-end balance because the money is already floating. That's all we want to establish as a baseline.)

To recall, former senator Antonio Trillanes IV claimed that the Vice President did not declare millions in time deposit assets in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN) from 2007 to 2010 when she was Davao City vice mayor.
The former lawmaker said that, based on the research of his team, Sara Duterte had undeclared dollar and peso time deposits from 2007 until 2010.
He said the Vice President also did not declare a million dollars' worth of life insurance in her 2010 SALN.
Duterte's camp rejected the claims of Trillanes.
Duterte's spokesperson Salvador Paolo Panelo Jr. said Trillanes has been repeatedly lying about the vice president and her family for years.

"Since 2016, former Senator Antonio Trillanes IV has been peddling the same exhausted lies regarding Extrajudicial Killings (EJKs), fabricated drug links, imaginary unexplained wealth, baseless corruption allegations, and fictional China connections against the Duterte family," Panelo said in a statement. —AOL, GMA News

articles.title: Teodoro, Nafarrete push for stronger military presence in Palawan
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) chief General Antonio Nafarrete called for a stronger and sustained military presence in Palawan during their visit to…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 4:15pm

Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. and Armed Forces of the Philippines (AFP) chief General Antonio Nafarrete called for a stronger and sustained military presence in Palawan during their visit to the Western Command (WESCOM) in Puerto Princesa City.
Teodoro and Nafarrete visited WESCOM at Camp General Artemio Ricarte on Tuesday where they met with personnel and discussed the command’s operational requirements and defense posture.
“Palawan is the last frontier, right? Let’s make sure that it is the last frontier,” Teodoro said.
Teodoro said Palawan’s unique operating environment requires not only discipline and resolve but also creativity and innovation from military personnel.

For him, it is important to set up a significant tri-service presence in the area to support territorial defense, internal security operations, humanitarian assistance and disaster response, as well as deterrence against unlawful activities.
Teodoro said the government is working to strengthen the presence and capabilities of the Philippine Army and Philippine Marine Corps in Palawan.
This includes establishing at least a brigade-sized Army presence and developing a sustainable growth plan for the Marine Corps.
He said the Marine Corps needs mobility to maintain its firepower and operational effectiveness, particularly along the eastern seaboard where there is currently no significant military presence.

Meanwhile, Nafarrete also stressed the need for sustained military presence, operational readiness and strengthened capabilities in the country's western frontiers “to effectively safeguard the country’s sovereignty and territorial integrity.”

The AFP said the visit reaffirmed its commitment to strengthening WESCOM and supporting its personnel as they perform their mandate of protecting the country's sovereignty and territorial integrity. — RSJ, GMA News

articles.title: Police routinely failing to investigate ‘revenge porn’ reports, research shows
articles.summary:
Lawyers launch super-complaint after gathering evidence suggesting officers frequently dismiss image-based abuse

Police forces are routinely failing to investigate complaints about the…

blocks.text: Police forces are routinely failing to investigate complaints about the circulation of image-based abuse, previously known as “revenge pornography”, according to research that has triggered a super-complaint over the way such crimes are handled.

Lawyers have gathered evidence from 100 people who reported intimate images being shared online without their consent. Their research suggests that image-based abuse is still frequently dismissed or not recognised as criminal offending, despite being described by the former prime minister Keir Starmer as a national emergency.

Referrals to the Revenge Porn helpline, the charity that helps victims get non-consensual images removed from the internet, increased by more than 4,000% between 2015 and 2025, but data from 39 police forces in England and Wales shows that charges were lodged against perpetrators in an average of just 4.5% of cases last year. In some forces the figure was lower than 1%.

Some police officers responded inappropriately when women tried to register complaints, researchers found. One reported that the officer “almost giggled on the phone to me”, while another said the officer responded: “Boys will be boys.” Another said: “I bet you’ve learned your lesson.”
Image-based abuse overwhelmingly affects women and girls, who make up 98.9% of reported images.

Lawyers from Leigh Day and the charity the Centre for Women’s Justice are working with the charity #NotYourPorn to highlight systemic police failings in responding to image-based abuse, defined as “the taking, sharing or creating of intimate content without the survivor’s consent, or threatening to do so”.
They note that rapid innovations in AI are helping abusers find new ways to create and disseminate synthetic explicit material, sometimes known as deepfake content.

Their research classifies the policing response as “fragmented, inconsistent and incapable of meeting the scale of the threat posed by image-based abuse”. “Despite the increased public awareness, and the creation of new criminal offences designed to address this conduct, there has been no corresponding increase in charging rates, prosecutions or convictions,” the complaint says.
“The unavoidable conclusion is that the overwhelming majority of this offending goes unaddressed.”
Home Office data shows that there were only 569 charges issued for image-based abuse in 2025/2026. The Revenge Porn Helpline received almost 25,000 reports in 2025.

Researchers found that the vast majority of survivors of image-based abuse did not report it to the police, noting that “embarrassment, shame and fear” contributed to their reluctance. Police outsourced the evidence-gathering process to survivors in many cases, the report notes, leaving them to work out how to collate proof that the images were being disseminated widely and how to get the content removed from the internet.

“It felt like to them it wasn’t a priority, it wasn’t even a crime,” one woman told researchers. Another said: “Police involvement has not alleviated the harm caused by this offence. Instead, it has intensified my distress and left me feeling powerless and completely unsupported as a victim.”

A police super-complaint is a mechanism introduced in 2018 to allow concerns to be raised about ways in which the police operate that may significantly harm the interests of the public generally, rather than focusing on an individual force of officer.
The complaint will be jointly considered by the College of Policing and the Independent Office for Police Conduct, which will decide whether to respond by opening a wider investigation.

Harriet Bland, a lawyer with the Centre for Women’s Justice, said: “Without an urgent overhaul of police guidance and training on image-based abuse – which must be regularly updated – and a clear national strategy rolled out across forces, survivors will continue to be let down.”

articles.title: Should kids living with obesity be on GLP-1s? New global guidance says yes — in some cases
articles.summary: The first-ever international guidelines on managing childhood obesity are raising the profile of GLP-1 treatments for kids and teens — but with strict criteria and a high degree of caution.

image.caption: The World Health Organization on Wednesday released its first-ever international guidelines on managing childhood obesity. (Ben Nelms/CBC)

blocks.text: The first-ever international guidelines on managing childhood obesity from the World Health Organization (WHO) are raising the profile of GLP-1 treatments for kids and teens — but with strict criteria and a high degree of caution.

The new global guidance, released on Wednesday, recommends a broad range of interventions to manage diet, boost physical activity and change behaviours for the rising number of global youth living with obesity. And in certain cases, for some older children and teenagers, that could also mean medication or bariatric surgery.
The WHO doesn't recommend medical treatment, surgery or weight-loss devices for children up to the age of nine, the organization notes.

For older youth from the age of 10 to 19, medical treatments may be considered only when a supervised lifestyle program hasn't achieved results, the guidance states, while bariatric surgery should only be an option under strict conditions for youth living with severe obesity.

"The foundation of obesity care for children and adolescents is not medicine or surgery, but access to comprehensive support that enables healthy eating, physical activity and sustainable behaviour change," said Dr. Luz María De Regil, the WHO's director of the department of nutrition and food safety.
Cheaper GLP-1s arrive in Canada: Are they safe?
London, Ont.-based pediatric endocrinologist Dr. Marina Ybarra welcomed the organization's cautious acknowledgement of medications as one avenue to tackle obesity.

Here in Canada, two GLP-1s are approved for weight management for youth aged 12 and up, but young patients typically have to pay for the drugs through their parents' insurance or out of pocket, said Ybarra, who works with Western University and leads the London Health Sciences Centre Children's Hospital pediatric weight management clinic.

items: Obesity Canada launches partnership aimed at improving care in health system

blocks.text: "The news about WHO encouraging GLP-1 as a possible treatment for children living with obesity — I think it's very good news," she said.
"Because maybe that will help us to get funding through the public system in Canada for children living with obesity. That's my biggest hope."
170 million youth living with obesity
The WHO's new guidance is meant to tackle skyrocketing rates of obesity among global youth.

Roughly 170 million children and teens around the world between the ages of five to 19 were living with obesity in 2024, the WHO noted. Obesity prevalence in this age group has also quadrupled since 1990, rising from two to eight per cent.

The global recommendations echo recent Canadian guidance to manage obesity in children. That long-awaited 2025 update also called for behavioural and psychological support and, in some cases, additional medical or surgical interventions.

items: How family doctors navigate the rise of weight loss drugs
Can GLP-1s curb more than your desire for food?

blocks.text: But Canadian physicians recommend only using GLP-1s to manage obesity in children after the age of 12, two years above the WHO's cutoff due, and don't stipulate that medical intervention should only be tried after lifestyle changes.

"There is no evidence to support a stepwise approach whereby pharmacologic and surgical interventions should be offered only if behavioural and psychological interventions prove ineffective," reads the guidance published in the Canadian Medical Association Journal.
"Using shared decision-making with families, health care providers should consider all intervention options."

The WHO, in contrast, focused on the "practicality and universality" of diet, physical activity and behavioural changes as the pillars of obesity management, and it stressed the need for "structured long-term follow-up" in cases where patients use medication alongside other lifestyle interventions.
Weight comes back quickly after quitting GLP-1 drugs: study
Caution around GLP-1 use among children

GLP-1s and other similar medications — known by household brand names like Ozempic, Mounjaro, Rybelsus, Wegovy and Zepbound — have exploded in popularity among adults to treat obesity and diabetes, and for general weight loss, even without a clear medical need.
The drugs work by mimicking the body's glucagon-like peptide-1 hormone, which helps manage appetite, slow digestion and regulate blood sugar.
Ybarra stressed the medications are now an effective tool for many young patients with obesity, helping to both reduce weight and improve quality of life.

items: 1st generic semaglutide injection for weight loss approved: Health Canada

blocks.text: While some children and teens face similar side effects to older patients, including nausea and other gastrointestinal issues, "we didn't see many of the severe complications that were seen in the adult population," Ybarra noted.
Younger and younger patients are also trying this growing class of drugs.

One U.S. study, published in the medical journal Pediatrics in September, revealed a 310-fold increase in GLP-1 prescriptions for children ages eight to 11, shooting up from 0.03 per cent to more than nine per cent between 2019 and 2026 — though overall use in this younger group remains rare.

items: Should everyone be on GLP-1s? What the science really tells us about cancer prevention and other benefits

blocks.text: Still, the WHO stressed the need for caution regarding GLP-1 use among children and teens, given limited research and the potential for misuse among certain groups, such as athletes or patients with eating disorders.

The WHO's new guidelines note that overall evidence linked to various medication treatments for childhood obesity, including GLP-1s and other drugs such as metformin or sibutramine, was "generally of low quality due to short term follow-up and evaluation, and [due to] the small numbers of studies and participants."
Ybarra agreed there's a lack of long-term data for the use of GLP-1s among youth, given how new these drugs are for younger patients.
"The data we have though, it's very reassuring and helpful — in terms of there's more benefits than risks."
GLP-1s and cancer prevention: What’s known and what isn’t
Drug trials underway for younger kids

As for the line in the sand regarding children under 10 avoiding GLP-1s, the WHO's María De Regil stressed in a Tuesday news conference that the agency "recommends prioritizing other interventions in this age group."
"However, it is clear that the research is going in this area," she said. "Some national pediatric associations may recommend it."

items: Serena Williams’ return to tennis sparks conversation about GLP-1 drugs in sports

blocks.text: Denmark's Novo Nordisk and U.S.-based Eli Lilly are among the drug makers currently trialling pediatric obesity medications for kids as young as six, though María De Regil wouldn’t speculate on how any of those ongoing trials might change the WHO's recommendations.
Major questions still remain about how children should safely use these types of drugs, and for how long, stressed María De Regil.
"We realize that this is a rapidly evolving field," she said.

articles.title: Immigration minister appears unaware of court ruling that guarantees Charter rights for refugees
articles.summary: Refugee rights advocates say they are shocked to hear that the federal immigration minister appeared in an interview with Radio-Canada to be unfamiliar with the landmark Supreme Court decision widely…

image.caption: In an interview with Radio-Canada, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab was repeatedly asked about the landmark 1985 Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration decision. She appeared to be unfamiliar with the case. (The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Politics·New

Refugee rights advocates say they are shocked to hear that the federal immigration minister appeared in an interview with Radio-Canada to be unfamiliar with the landmark Supreme Court decision widely considered to be the cornerstone of the Canadian refugee protection system.
Supreme Court's landmark Singh decision led to establishment of Refugee Board

Refugee rights advocates say they are shocked that the federal immigration minister appeared to be unfamiliar with the landmark Supreme Court decision widely considered to be the cornerstone of the Canadian refugee protection system.
In an interview with Radio-Canada, Immigration Minister Lena Metlege Diab was repeatedly asked about the 1985 Singh v. Minister of Employment and Immigration case.
This Singh decision ruled that asylum seekers are guaranteed the Charter right to fundamental justice and led to the creation of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada.
It is also a key argument in the legal challenge to the Carney government's immigration reforms that restrict who is eligible for Refugee Board hearings.

items: 'You are a very bad minister,' immigration critic says at tense meeting
Canadians born abroad caught up in citizenship certificate delays

blocks.text: "Honestly, I was extremely shocked," said Gauri Sreenivasan, co-executive director of the Canadian Council for Refugees. "It's very concerning that the minister in charge of Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada would not be fully aware of the Supreme Court's Singh decision."
Diab was interviewed in July by Radio-Canada's Les murs: le périple des migrants vers le Canada, a documentary podcast launched three weeks ago that examines Canada's asylum system.
She was asked a series of questions, including about the Safe Third Country Agreement and Bill C-12, the Carney government's immigration reforms passed last March.

One of the most controversial changes in C-12 was that asylum claims made more than a year after an individual's first entry into Canada are no longer referred to the Refugee Board, but instead are given a pre-removal risk assessment.

The assessment is conducted by an Immigration Canada officer to ensure that a person is not at risk of being tortured or killed if returned to their country — and typically includes a written submission rather than an oral hearing.
Migrant rights rally calls on government to change immigration policy
Diab said in French that Bill C-12 "respects our Canadian Charter," adding that she herself is a lawyer and that the changes are meant to address the backlog in asylum cases.

When pressed about the argument that under the Singh decision asylum seekers have a constitutional right to an oral hearing, she replied that since the law is new, the government would continue to monitor the situation.
Radio-Canada then asked her point-blank if she was familiar with the Singh decision. After a pause, Diab asked that the name of the decision be repeated.
When told again that it was the Singh decision handed down by the Supreme Court of Canada in 1985, she said she would have to check with her team.
"There are many Singhs and many decisions," said Diab.
Immigration minister asked about court ruling that guarantees Charter rights for refugees
Radio-Canada then specified that it was the decision that led to the creation of the Refugee Board, to which she responded: "Ah, OK."
With the Singh decision, the Supreme Court of Canada recognized, among other things, the right of asylum seekers to an oral hearing, according to several experts Radio-Canada spoke with.

"[The claimant] is entitled to a full hearing on their file so that they can explain their situation before a competent decision-maker," said François Crépeau, professor emeritus of public international law at McGill University and former United Nations special rapporteur on the human rights of migrants.
"That is why the Immigration and Refugee Board was created in 1989. It was to meet the requirements of the Singh decision."
Bill C-12 is being challenged in the courts. Lawyers allege it violates Canada's legal obligations under both domestic and international law.

items: Canada's new asylum law puts Iranians in limbo
Where is Canada's immigration minister? Community groups are asking

blocks.text: Immigration Canada maintains that the Singh decision is respected by Bill C-12.

"The Supreme Court in Singh found that in order to meet the requirements of fundamental justice, an oral hearing is required when there is a credibility issue at stake. The Supreme Court did not find that in all cases an oral hearing is required," a department lawyer told a parliamentary committee studying Bill C-12 in February.
Crépeau disagrees: "Removing a full hearing … is a violation of the conditions set by the Singh decision."
Immediately after the interview, Diab's office insisted that the minister was well aware of the Singh decision, but that due to the language barrier she had not fully understood the questions.
The podcast interview was conducted in French, which is not Diab's first language.

However, during two appearances in English before two different Senate committees studying Bill C-12, the minister also did not answer questions regarding the Singh decision, deferring to department officials and lawyers.
'Issue of competence': advocate
"I believe there is certainly an issue of competence," said Louis-Philippe Jannard of TCRI, a Quebec umbrella association of more than 160 organizations working with refugees and immigrants.

"The issue of the Singh decision was raised during the legislative process for Bill C-12 before both the House of Commons and the Senate. So for it not to be on the minister's radar is surprising to say the least."
Radio-Canada asked the Prime Minister's Office (PMO) whether, given these criticisms, Diab still has the confidence of Prime Minister Mark Carney.

PMO spokesperson Renée LeBlanc Proctor said in an email to Radio-Canada that Diab plays an "essential" role in the implementation of the federal government's mandate to bring down immigration to "viable" levels while attracting the best talent in the world.
"She continues this work," Proctor said.

Diab was previously criticized by immigrant rights groups who said the minister was hard to reach and did not seem to have a firm grasp of her cabinet portfolio. The Opposition Conservatives have been calling for Diab to be fired for months.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Brigitte Bureau is an award-winning investigative reporter with Radio-Canada. You can reach her by email: brigitte.bureau@radio-canada.ca.

articles.title: What's the fire danger from lithium batteries?
articles.summary: Firefighters have raised alarms about hot, fast, hard-to-extinguish fires in lithium batteries from e-bikes in people's homes and huge storage batteries at a P.E.I. solar farm. Here's why lithium…

image.caption: A 2024 e-bike fire in a Toronto subway car led to a seasonal e-bike transit ban. Lithium batteries, especially from e-bikes, are a growing cause of fires across Canada.

blocks.text: Firefighters have raised alarms about hot, fast, hard-to-extinguish fires in lithium batteries from e-bikes in people's homes (including one in Toronto just this week) and huge storage batteries at a P.E.I. solar farm last month.

Concerns about lithium battery fires have led to bans of electric bikes and cars in some buildings, public transit and ferries, causing problems for people who rely on them. They've also made some people hesitant about trying electric vehicles.
This week is Fire Prevention Week, and lithium batteries are the official theme. Here's a closer look at why lithium battery fires are a challenge and what can be done to minimize the risks.
Why lithium-ion batteries are so dangerous
How common are lithium battery fires?

Canadian fire departments don't track them in a consistent way, but a survey from the Canadian Association of Fire Chiefs estimates there were 1,500 fires started by lithium batteries in 600 communities across the country last year. Their numbers are growing exponentially with the numbers of lithium battery-powered devices, says Paul Boissoneault, president of the association and chief of the Oakville Fire Department.
Lithium battery fires are most common for devices found in people's homes, especially e-bikes and e-scooters.

EV and energy storage batteries are far rarer, as they're rigorously tested and have built-in safety features like temperature sensors and systems that cool battery cells as needed. Canada-wide statistics on EV fires aren't available, although U.S. data suggests they're extremely uncommon compared to fires in gas-powered vehicles.
LISTEN | Separating fact from fiction about EV battery fires:
What On Earth28:30Separating fact from fiction about EV battery fires
Grid storage battery fires are even less common — a global database from the Electric Power Research Institute shows the one in P.E.I. was one of only six worldwide this year.

items: As Summerside works to contain fire at solar farm, this expert says such fires are rare

blocks.text: What causes lithium battery fires?
Batteries rely on the separation of their positive and negative terminals. That forces electrons to move through the device you're powering to get from one end of the battery to the other.

A barrier material keeps the terminals separated. When a hole (effectively a short circuit) forms in that barrier, fire happens, said Randy Narine, a professional firefighter in Brampton, Ont., who studies lithium battery safety through his company Clean Core Research, in an interview with CBC's What on Earth?
That hole can be caused by wear and tear over time or from damage, such as a collision or someone dropping a battery from a smaller device, such as an e-bike.

Lithium battery fires can also be started from overheating — due to overcharging or improper charging (such as with the wrong charger) or heat exposure from an external heat source, including a fire in a nearby battery cell in the same battery, since many batteries contain multiple cells.
Regina fire chief gives reminder to check charging devices
What makes them dangerous compared to other fires?

They can burn "hotter and faster" than other fires, Boissoneault said. At a certain temperature, lithium batteries reach "thermal runaway," where heat triggers and speeds up chemical reactions in the battery that generate more heat.
This can lead to a "massive chain reaction" and a potentially explosive fire, Narine said.

They make their own oxygen. One of the battery's terminals is made of a metal oxide that breaks down into metal and oxygen gas during a fire, further sustaining the fire. That means normal techniques to smother fires don't work.

They generate toxic substances such as hydrogen fluoride as materials in the battery break down in the heat. They can also contaminate firefighters' clothing and equipment with toxic compounds such as formaldehyde and heavy metals that need to be removed afterward.

They can reignite hours, days or weeks later, thanks to thermal runaway and their oxygen self-generation. Boissoneault said that can have implications for how the burned batteries are transported and stored after a fire.
The fire at this P.E.I. solar farm is finally out. Officials warn it could reignite

Firefighters don't always feel prepared for them. Boissoneault said just 40 per cent of departments surveyed had formal training on dealing with lithium battery incidents, and even fewer said they had standard operating policies and the correct equipment to deal with such emergencies. Many also don't have a way to decontaminate their gear after a lithium fire.
How can they be handled and extinguished?

EV fires are typically sprayed with huge amounts of water. Narine estimated a gas car fire can be extinguished with less than 2,000 litres of water, whereas it can take tens of thousands of litres to put out a lithium battery fire.
While water can provide cooling and can sometimes be used to protect nearby materials from catching fire, it can't actually smother the battery fire.
Why has a battery been burning for nearly 2 weeks at Summerside's solar farm?
In many cases, fire experts say, the fire just needs to burn out.
That's particularly the case for large energy storage batteries, said experts at a fire safety panel at the Energy Storage Canada conference in Toronto in September.

Adam Jakubowski, a firefighter and senior consultant with Energy Safety Response Group specializing in battery energy storage systems, said in many cases, putting water on a lithium battery fire simply prolongs a fire, which may reignite a week or month later. It can also lead to water runoff that could contaminate the environment.
Toronto's fire chief calls e-bike batteries the 'greatest public fire safety risk'
What can you do to reduce the risk?
Buy batteries with certification labels such as CSA, cUL or CETL rather than cheaper ones that may not have safety features. Don't modify batteries to charge more quickly or hold more charge.

Charge devices properly, on hard surfaces, away from any combustible materials, and unplug as soon as they're fully charged, Boissoneault says. Charge with the right charger for that device. "Don't mix and match," says Jon McQuaid, vice-president of marketing communications and safety for Call2Recycle Canada, a non-profit focused on battery collection and recycling.

Recycle them only at battery-recycling dropoff sites, not trash or regular recycling bins, McQuaid said. He advises taping over the terminals (even for tiny button batteries) first to protect from debris or other batteries that could cause a spark, "which could then lead to a thermal runaway."
Damaged batteries need to be placed in special "damaged, defective or recalled" battery containers at select battery dropoff sites.
What can you do to prevent a lithium-ion battery fire in your home?

articles.title: On day one, rush for GCash IPO shares briefly trips up trading systems
articles.summary: 'I heard some platforms went down because of the traffic. That’s a good problem for all of us, right?' Mynt president and CEO Martha Sazon tells a room full of potential GCash investors hours after…

blocks.text: READY. The scene before GCash executives take the stage to sell the crowd on GCash on October 6, 2026.
Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler

'I heard some platforms went down because of the traffic. That’s a good problem for all of us, right?' Mynt president and CEO Martha Sazon tells a room full of potential GCash investors hours after the public offer formally opened

items: Mynt's executives presented a polished pitch to investors for GCash's IPO, highlighting strong demand and oversubscription from both retail and institutional investors.
The initial proposed share price was P10, but the final offer was set at P6.60, which is significantly lower and reflects a more justified valuation based on earnings projections.
GCash, as the leading e-wallet in the Philippines, is expected to focus on expanding its services beyond just user growth, including lending and overseas expansion.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

It was a polished courtship of the people being asked to hand over billions of pesos for a piece of GCash. Mynt’s top executives and a troop of underwriters took turns selling investors on the company’s growth story, while food and drinks flowed around the room.

Mynt president and CEO Martha Sazon took the stage, speaking before a packed room of investors, brokers, and bankers in Makati on Tuesday, October 6, just hours after the public offer for GCash’s parent company formally opened.
“We see a lot of buzz and a lot of activities,” Sazon said. “I heard some platforms went down because of the traffic. That’s a good problem for all of us, right?”

And amid all the hype and marketing, there is some truth to the matter too. A screenshot seen by Rappler showed a user attempting to enter GStocks PH through the GCash app before being redirected toward InvestaTrade, the online trading platform offered by AB Capital Securities.
The screen displayed an error saying there was a “problem communicating with GCash API at the moment.”
Sources close to the incident told Rappler that the disruption was brief and that the platform was back up again shortly afterward.
But if anything, all this goes to show that demand for the homegrown champion is, apparently, red-hot.

An analyst at a prominent local brokerage told Rappler Tuesday that its allocation was already oversubscribed, meaning client orders had exceeded the shares available through the brokerage. In such cases, investors may receive fewer shares than they requested, depending on the final allocation.

Even before the retail offer began, institutional investors had already piled in. Mynt said on October 2 that its institutional bookbuilding was multiple times oversubscribed, with demand going beyond commitments from more than 20 cornerstone investors.

At P6.60 per share, Mynt is selling around 8.03 billion shares worth approximately P53 billion. That remains below Monde Nissin’s more than P55-billion IPO in 2021, but Mynt also has an overallotment option covering another 1.20 billion secondary shares.
If fully exercised, the deal could raise as much as P60.9 billion and become the largest initial public offering (IPO) in Philippine history.

blocks.caption: PSE enters new territory with GCash’s IPO. But to thrive, it must go further.

blocks.text: The audience, meanwhile, had plenty of questions for GCash. Among them was whether the current price was even the right price at all.

When the PSE approved Mynt’s listing application in September, the company initially proposed to sell shares at up to P10 each. The exchange made clear at the time that this was a maximum price and that the final offer price would only be determined after bookbuilding.
“It was an administrative up to offer price that is required as part of the Philippines listing application, which is different from listing application processes in other countries,”
The eventual P6.60 price was 34% below that ceiling.
Mynt chief financial officer Evelyn Ng pushed back against the idea that the company had started out expecting investors to pay P10.
“P10 was never the price that we expected to list Mynt,” Ng told the room.

blocks.caption: PANEL. GCash executives line up for a question and answer session with the crowd following the investor briefing on October 6, 2026. Photo by Lance Spencer Yu/Rappler.

blocks.text: “It was an administrative ‘up to’ offer price that is required as part of the Philippines listing application, which is different from listing application processes in other countries,” she added.
Mynt then went through investor meetings and bookbuilding, with input from the company, selling shareholders, prospective investors, and its banking advisers before arriving at P6.60.
That said, is P6.60 the right price? The offer is easier to justify than the original P10 ceiling.

At P10, Mynt would have been valued at roughly P669 billion, or nearly 39 times its 2025 earnings. At P6.60, that falls to about P442 billion and around 25.6 times 2025 earnings, which is still a hefty premium for the local market.

Investors also have to consider what they are buying into. GCash is already the dominant e-wallet, so any future gains will likely have to come from lending, investments, insurance, merchants, and overseas expansion rather than simply adding more wallet users.
Around 80% of the base offer is also made up of secondary shares being sold by existing shareholders, rather than fresh capital going to Mynt. – Rappler.com

articles.title: UK house prices flatline as rising mortgage costs weigh on market
articles.summary: Average cost of home in September was £298,441, says Lloyds – about the same as year earlier and in August

blocks.text: UK house prices flatlined in September, according to a leading index, as rising mortgage costs started to weigh on the market.
The average cost of a home was £298,441, roughly the same as it was a year earlier and in the previous month, according to the tracker from Lloyds previously known as the Halifax HPI.
Economists polled by Reuters had predicted a 0.1% monthly rise in prices, according to the median forecast, as well as a 0.2% annual increase.

It came after house prices fell by 0.3% in August, the first decline in three years, as prospective buyers were hit by geopolitical uncertainty, combined with higher mortgage rates and stretched affordability.

In recent weeks most big banks and building societies have put prices up as a result of turmoil in the global bond markets, even though there has not been a change in the Bank of England base rate since December last year.

Andrew Asaam, the mortgages director at Lloyds, said: “While the market overall has been fairly subdued, property prices have so far proved resilient during a period of higher mortgage rates, which has been driven by changing expectations around the future path of base rate.”

On Monday the average cost of a five-year fixed-rate mortgage reached 6% for the first time in three years. Rising mortgage rates are bad news for borrowers whose fixed-rate deals are ending, as well as prospective buyers who are hoping to take out a mortgage to buy a home and the sellers who want the best price from them.
It also adds to the squeeze facing consumers as a result of higher energy bills, linked to the Iran war, while rising prices elsewhere are raising concerns of a new cost of living crisis.

Asaam said: “While higher mortgage rates and wider economic uncertainty are encouraging some people to take a more measured approach, new inquiries from prospective buyers are now at their highest since February.”
He added that any movement in house prices was likely to remain modest.
after newsletter promotion

Tom Bill, the head of UK residential research at the estate agent Knight Frank, said: “This year has been a story of rising energy prices and stalling house prices, as the unpredictable Middle East conflict unfolds and drives borrowing costs higher. This month’s budget adds to the uncertainty as buyers and sellers wonder which of the recurring tax rumours proves to be true.”

The number of people applying for a mortgage to buy a property fell between July and September, as higher borrowing costs continued to affect prospective housebuyers’ budgets, according to quarterly figures from Stonebridge, one of the UK’s largest independent mortgage and protection networks.

Mortgage applications for home purchases fell by 18.2% in the third quarter compared with a year earlier, Stonebridge found, while applications from first-time buyers slumped 18.6% over the same period.
However, rising numbers of applications for remortgaging helped to slow the decline in overall mortgage activity.

articles.title: At least 11 dead, 34 injured after ‘vile’ attack on Ukraine on Putin’s birthday, Zelenskyy says – Europe live
articles.summary:
Ukraine president confirms series of attacks on Pryluky, Dnipro, Kremenchik, Zaporizhzhia and Kyiv

Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched “one fo the most vile…

blocks.text: At least 11 dead, 34 injured after 'vile' attack on Ukraine on Putin's birthday, Zelenskyy says

blocks.caption: Jakub Krupa

blocks.text: Jakub Krupa
Ukraine’s president Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Russia launched “one fo the most vile strikes” on Ukraine last night, targeting the country’s energy infrastructure overnight.

At least 11 people were killed, and more than 34 injured in a series of attacks on Pryluky, Dnipro, Kremenchik, Zaporizhzhia, and Kyiv, which Zelenskyy ironically called “a birthday gift for Putin” who turns 74 today.

blocks.caption: Rescuers work at a site of an apartment building damaged by a Russian missile strike in the town of Pryluky, Chernihiv region, Ukraine. Photograph: State Emergency Service Of Ukraine/Reuters

blocks.text: “Russian ballistic missiles remain the greatest challenge. And air defense packages for us right now are a vital necessity. That is why every day we are looking for missiles for Patriot systems that can and must actually protect people’s lives here, in Ukrainian skies,” Zelenskyy said.
Ukraine’s foreign minister Andrii Sybiha went further, saying:
“On Putin’s birthday, Russian generals brought him his favorite present: war crimes.”
He added:

“What Russian generals fail to tell Putin is that he is not winning this war and never will. … I urge all partners to give Putin real presents that will help him finally choose diplomacy over war. Stronger sanctions on his military-industrial complex, including facilities producing ballistic missiles and the Rassvet satellite system, as well as stronger support for Ukraine, including all kinds of air defense and energy assistance ahead of winter. But his ultimate present will be a dock in The Hague. We are preparing the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression Against Ukraine for practical launch already next year. Putin and his friends should know that accountability is inevitable.”

Elsewhere, I will bring you the latest from France, as high school protests continue after a major march in Paris, which ended with sporadic vandalism and running skirmishes with riot police, and officers firing teargas and carrying out baton charges to disperse protesters.

Following allegations of police brutality, interior minister Laurent Nuñez suspended the use of stun grenades at the protests, after a 15-year-old reportedly lost a hand on Monday, and a 14-year old lost several teeth.
The French PM, Sébastien Lecornu, is expected to speak later today to set out his plans for responding to the protests.
I will bring you also all other news from across Europe.
It’s Wednesday, 7 October 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.
Good morning.

articles.title: Nicolas Ghesquière takes us into the future for Louis Vuitton show in Paris
articles.summary:
Models walk runway at the Louvre with flying cars hovering above as designer envisions city life in a warming world

In silk slip dresses, breezy vented tunics and gossamer layers of chiffon,…

blocks.text: In silk slip dresses, breezy vented tunics and gossamer layers of chiffon, the models on Louis Vuitton’s catwalk were perfectly dressed for an unseasonably warm October evening in Paris. As the show began at sunset it was still 24C.
This summer’s record temperatures were on designer Nicolas Ghesquiière’s mind. “The world is getting warmer, this definitely had a strong influence” he said.

The show was staged in an inner courtyard of the Louvre, the catwalk illuminated by the tail lights of a fleet of 34 flying cars in Vuitton’s signature Damier check raised on stilts above the catwalk.

blocks.caption: Models on the runway. Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni / WWD / Getty Images

blocks.text: The contrast between the futuristic set and the historic buildings was an elegant echo of the centrepiece of the Louvre, where IM Pei’s glass pyramid stands amid the French classical architecture.

blocks.caption: Nicolas Ghesquière. Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: The future is always on Ghesquière’s mind – his science fiction bent showed up in the models’ beaded silver fringes that were somewhere between space-age hair extensions and sun visors – and this season, he was thinking about life in the cities of the future, his models as pedestrians among flying cars. “I was thinking about a woman walking through traffic, and how in the urban environment we sometimes feel vulnerable and sometimes feel strong.”

The featherlight fabrics and free-floating silhouettes were a departure from the angular, ornate looks which are his signature. “I am a specialist in a kind of fashion that is like armour, fashion with strong architecture, but this summer I think we all felt like we needed a different wardrobe. The world is getting warmer. We need to think differently, for clothes to be relevant today and in the future.”

Zendaya wore a ruffled organza jacket last seen on her Odyssey press tour and the Rivals actor Bella Maclean was in sleek black tailoring. Ghesquière took his bow casually dressed in jeans – but then, the show was only his second most important moment of Paris fashion week. Louis Vuitton is the flagship brand of luxury giant LVMH, which contributes about 1% to French GDP, placing it close to the core of economic and cultural power in Paris.

blocks.caption: Zendaya she arrives for the Louis Vuitton show. Photograph: Lou Benoist/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: On Friday Ghesquière, who has led Vuitton for a decade, was knighted by President Emmanuel Macron for his contribution to French creative industries, at a ceremony at the Élysée Palace.
after newsletter promotion

The first lady, Brigitte Macron, has a longstanding close collaboration with Ghesquière, attending his shows and wearing custom looks for state occasions. President Macron began his speech joking that “it feels strange to be decorating someone tonight who is used to looking at my wife from every angle … she just told me you are the second man in her life.”

blocks.caption: A model on the Louis Vuitton runway. Photograph: Giovanni Giannoni/WWD/Getty Images

blocks.text: Guests at the ceremony reflected the broad reach of Louis Vuitton, with Catherine Deneuve and the British designer Phoebe Philo alongside K-pop star Felix of Stray Kids. Ghesquière wore a striking double-breasted Louis Vuitton black suit, with a single button fastening and no lapel. Pinning the red ribboned medallion to his chest, Macron said: “This evening … it is the Republic itself that is adding a new element to your wardrobe.”

articles.title: The solar boom is rapidly transforming emerging economies
articles.summary: Renewable electricity is cheaper than ever. So while the West got rich on coal and oil, some of the poorest countries in the world are banking on solar, wind and water instead.

image.caption: Solar panels are becoming a common sight in rural parts of Ethiopia. Farmers who previously used diesel generators for irrigation are switching to solar power, like here in the village Dore Bafeno in the Sidama region in 2026.Image: Shewangizaw Wegayehu/DW

blocks.text: As emerging economies and global standards of living grow, is the world in for another fossil fuel boom? The data says not. Countries from Southeast Asia to Sub-Saharan Africa aren't investing in fossil fuels like the West did, but in electricity, powered by renewables.

When the US and Europe industrialized in the 19th and 20th century, they did so using fossil energy. From coal ovens, gas heating and combustion engine cars to electricity produced in coal and gas power plants, entire societies relied on polluting sources of fuel.
Yet while burning fossil fuels allowed industrialized countries to boom, it also caused the climate crisis that is linked to extreme weather events around the world today.
Renewable electricity is rapidly becoming the cheapest option
Many of the same countries that became economically powerful off the back of fossil fuels are now trying to transition to renewables. But they are held back by centuries of legacy infrastructure.

Because a gas boiler won't run on wind power, and a diesel truck cannot be solar-powered, societies looking to shift to green energy need to use more electricity and increase their share of renewables.

That is where many middle- and lower-income countries have an advantage. With less existing energy infrastructure built around fossil fuels, they are better placed for a faster rollout of renewable electricity sources.

In many instances, solar power in particular is now cheaper to produce than fossil electricity. And unlike large coal or gas plants, which take years to construct and millions in investments, solar and wind farms can be built quickly and with much less upfront cost.

At the same time, according to an analysis by renewables think tank Ember, electronic devices like refrigerators, electric stoves or air conditioners have all become much cheaper in the last decades, making electricity a more affordable option as an energy source for cooking, heating and more.

While electric cars are still a luxury item in most places, their prices are coming down too. And a UN study found that in India, Indonesia and Vietnam electric scooters and motorbikes already cost the same as petrol models. Yet a lot less to fuel.
All this means that renewable electricity is quickly becoming the best choice for the wallet — not just for the climate. And countries are taking note.

"We're seeing a leapfrog take place right across the emerging markets,” said Kingsmill Bond, energy strategist at Ember. "The whole of Asia is electrifying quickly, and the whole of Europe and the United States is stagnant."
Lower-income countries are electrifying faster
In 2023, only around a quarter of global electricity was generated by renewables. But that figure is rising fast, and almost all new capacity added these days is based on solar or wind power.
Lower-income countries already use less fossil fuels and more renewables than higher-income ones.

And large middle-income economies are outpacing richer ones as well. In 2023, solar power alone made up at least six percent and ten percent of electricity in India and Vietnam respectively. The global average was five percent.
Lower-income countries are electrifying without the fossil detour

This boom has meant middle- and lower income countries are electrifying fast, consuming less energy directly from fossil fuels than richer countries. Vietnam, for instance, is already using more electric energy than the US, Europe and even China, and India is following the same path.
But the potential for energy leapfrogging might be particularly high in low-income countries, most of them across Sub-Saharan Africa.

Countries such as Kenya, Ethiopia or Namibia are expanding their energy infrastructure rapidly right now to meet the demands of a growing, young population. But rural areas in many countries are not connected to electricity grids.
And Joel Nana, project manager at South African NGO Sustainable Energy Africa says that "even when there is access to power, it's often not reliable.”

Until a few years ago, he says, people would default to diesel generators to fill their energy needs. But that came at a cost, because importing fuel is particularly expensive in many African countries, meaning energy crises and oil price fluctuations hit much harder.
Renewables for energy access and independence
These factors make solar power a solution for both energy access and independence. And it has become so cheap that Nana says it's a "no brainer”.

"Some businesses can make back their investment in just two years, so why would you want to deploy anything else?” he said. "Solar has rapidly become the de facto default technology that everyone falls back on.”

And once it is set up, it is very effective. Sub-Saharan Africa is extremely well-suited to solar power. It gets more sun than almost anywhere in the world, and has enough space for solar farms to cover electricity demand hundreds of times over.
"If you add solar plus batteries, you can get cheap electricity about 90 percent of the time from the sun alone”, said Kingsmill Bond.
Countries like Namibia, South Africa, Kenya and Senegal have expanded their solar capacity massively in the past few years.

In a 2026 report for African Tech Futures Lab and Ember, Nana analyzed import data from China and estimated that around 100,000 solar panels were installed across Africa every day in 2026, up 45 percent from just the previous year.

Similar trends are emerging all across the world. In Pakistan, for example, people have been buying solar panels from China en masse in the past few years to avoid steep electricity grid prices and frequent power outages.
Cheap energy boosts economies

Aleksi Lumijärvi, director for knowledge, policy and finance at the International Renewable Energy Association says these decisions can have a major impact on the global economy in the coming decades.
"Industrial companies will find that it will be cheaper to move production to, for example, somewhere in Sub-Saharan Africa, because they have this cheap, clean solar power plus batteries available.”
Kingsmill Bond says where electricity is cheap and abundant, wealth will follow.
"You're going to have faster growth in the emerging markets, you will have fewer financial crises. It will make a material difference to people's quality of lives.”
Nana says the next step for African countries is to establish policies that ensure everyone benefits from the solar boom.

"We are heading towards the most decentralized grid in the whole world within the next five years,” he told DW. His mantra for governments, he says, is: "This is happening, whether you like it or not.” He expects a wave of new energy regulations, many of which are now in the final stages of negotiation, to come into effect across Africa in the coming months and years.
"Countries are realizing it's in their interest to integrate this technology into national strategies, to share the benefits and to make use of this competitive advantage.”
All data and code behind this analysis can be found in this Github repository.
More data-driven stories by DW can be found here.

articles.title: COA disallows with finality OVP's P73M confidential funds release in December 2022
articles.summary: The Commission on Audit (COA) has affirmed with finality its notice of disallowance on the disbursement of P73 million in confidential funds by the Office of the Vice President from December 22 to…

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 3:33pm

The Commission on Audit (COA) has affirmed with finality its notice of disallowance on the disbursement of P73 million in confidential funds by the Office of the Vice President from December 22 to 31, 2022.

In a 15-page resolution, the commission said the OVP only submitted acknowledgment receipts to substantiate the confidential expenses and did not comply with the rules of the COA, the joint circular on the disbursement of confidential funds, and the national budget.
"They are, at best, a farce, of no significance, and utterly subpar the scintilla of substance which needed to demonstrate the proper disposal of the OVP's CF," the COA said.
GMA News Online has sought comment from the OVP and will publish it as soon as it is available.
The COA said a disbursement of large public funds deserves no less; taxpayers' money should always be spent with paramount consideration of full transparency and reasonable budget allocation.

"Indubitably, these cannot be wantonly sacrificed on the altar of exigency in as much as reckless handling and accounting of public funds have no place in a government that endeavors to keep inviolate the trust of the people," the COA said.

The motion for reconsideration of the notice of disallowance was filed by Vice President Sara Z. Duterte, OVP special disbursing officer Gina F. Acosta, and OVP chief accountant Julieta L. Villadelrey.
The COA, on August 8, 2024, issued a notice of disallowance on the confidential expenses of the OVP from December 2 to 31, 2022, in the amount of P73,287,000.
The commission, in a decision on April 10, 2026, affirmed the notice. The latest resolution affirmed the disallowance with finality.
The Joint Circular No. 2015-01 which governs the entitlement, release, use, reporting, and audit of confidential funds and intelligence funds.

The circular also states that as the utilization of such funds is confidential and classified by nature, it requires “strong internal controls” and “strict accounting and auditing rules to prevent mishandling or improper applications of the funds.” –NB, GMA News

articles.summary: Transport network companies (TNCs) were urged to speed up the development and implementation of the fixed pickup fare system in their ride-hailing services, a digital advocates group pressed.

blocks.text: Published October 7, 2026 3:28pm
Transport network companies (TNCs) were urged to speed up the development and implementation of the fixed pickup fare system in their ride-hailing services, a digital advocates group pressed.

“While we recognize that technical adjustments may be necessary, we believe that implementation should not be unnecessarily delayed, particularly at a time when ride-hailing drivers are facing increasing operating costs, including higher fuel prices, whose impact is affecting the general public,” said Digital Pinoys in a statement on Wednesday.

In July, the Land Transportation Franchising and Regulatory Board (LTFRB) revived the fixed pick-up fare for transport network vehicle services (TNVS) to strike a balance between the concerns of TNVS drivers and commuters' complaints over unauthorized and unregulated pick-up charges.

The memorandum prohibits the collection of pick-up fares beyond a five-kilometer radius and directs TNCs to limit their matching radius to five kilometers to minimize passenger waiting times and drivers' operating costs.
The LTFRB earlier summoned 19 ride-hailing services for defying the fare hike implementation.
Moreover, Digital Pinoys noted that when fare structure does not adequately account for the cost of providing a trip, drivers may become less willing to accept certain bookings.
“This can result in increased non-acceptance and cancellation of trips, ultimately affecting commuters who depend on motorcycle taxis for their daily transportation,” the group said.
But Digital Pinoys emphasized that passengers should understand that the fare adjustment is needed by the drivers amid the rising costs of operations.

“When drivers are able to earn reasonably from the trips they accept, they are more likely to remain available on the platform, resulting in better trip acceptance, fewer cancellations, and more applicable transportation for commuters,” said the group.
GMA News Online reached out to TNCs such as Grab and Angkas for their comments.
Follow facebook.com/gmanewsonline for real-time news and developments in the Philippines and around the world.—Vince Angelo Ferreras/RF, GMA News

articles.title: ‘Lawyers should be running to courts’ to stop coal approvals after landmark ruling, NSW MP says
articles.summary:
High court finding in favour of Hunter Valley community group sets precedent other environmentalists should follow, advocate says

A landmark decision in Australia’s first climate change high…
articles.byline: Donna Lu, Lisa Cox, and Adam Morton

blocks.text: A landmark decision in Australia’s first climate change high court case has been described as a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that exported greenhouse gas emissions “cannot simply be ignored”.

On Wednesday morning, the nation’s highest court ruled that the approval of MACH Energy’s Mount Pleasant coalmine expansion in NSW’s Hunter Valley was invalid, in a judgment that sets a precedent for fossil fuel projects in the state.

The coal company brought the high court case after a local community group, the Denman Aberdeen Muswellbrook Scone Healthy Environment Group (Dams Heg), halted the coalmine expansion on climate grounds in the NSW court of appeal.

In a 3-2 split ruling, the high court found the state’s Independent Planning Commission (IPC) failed to consider imposing conditions to minimise greenhouse gas emissions that would be generated by the mine when the coal is sold and burnt overseas. Known as scope 3 emissions, these are not counted in Australia’s domestic tally.

Commenting on the judgment, the deputy Greens leader, Steph Hodgins-May, said: “For too long, big coal and gas companies have tried to pretend that the emissions from their products are someone else’s problem once they leave Australian shores. They’re not.
“When Australian coal is burned overseas, the climate damage doesn’t magically disappear at the port. It comes back to communities here through worsening heat, drought, bushfires and floods.
“This judgment sends a clear message to governments and fossil fuel companies that the climate impacts of their projects cannot simply be ignored or pushed down the line.”

NSW Greens MP Sue Higginson, formerly a public interest environmental lawyer, also said the high court judgment could lead to “significant legal difficulty” for the Hunter Valley Operations (HVO) coalmine extension, which was approved by the IPC a week ago.

In greenlighting the HVO extension – the biggest in the state’s history – the IPC ruled that emissions from the mine would “contribute to climate change impacts on the people, economy and environment of the Hunter region, NSW and globally”, but that their impacts had been outweighed by economic benefits to the region.

For both the HVO and Mount Pleasant coal developments, 98% of the emissions were scope 3 emissions, Higginson said. “HVO’s environmental impact statement didn’t even account for scope 3 emissions at all, and the high court has been crystal clear that consent authorities must ensure emissions are minimised to the greatest extent practicable. It seems clear that the approval of HVO fails this test.
“Lawyers should be running to the courts right now with this judgment in hand, ready to stop coal approvals in their tracks,” she said.

In a joint statement, the Liberal leader, Angus Taylor, and the Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, described the decision as a threat to “Australia’s standing as a reliable energy exporter” and said the federal and NSW governments “must act immediately to fix the law”.
after newsletter promotion

“A project extension the Independent Planning Commission approved in 2022, after years of assessment, has been sent back to square one,” they said, arguing that the Minns government should amend NSW’s Environmental Planning and Assessment Act to “make clear that overseas emissions from Australia’s exported resources are not a consideration in project approvals”.
The climate change minister, Chris Bowen, who is in Fiji chairing climate negotiations, said: “The law of the land is law of the land, as interpreted by the high court, and we respect that.

“If others don’t, if others are so biased in their approach that they don’t respect the law of the land, that’s a matter for them. It says a bit about their approach, but that’s about as all I’m going to say because it’s a court case and I’m not in Australia at the moment.”

Murray Watt, the federal environment minister, said on Wednesday afternoon that while he had not had an opportunity to review the judgment in full, “the decision from the high court is in relation to a New South Wales government decision based on New South Wales legislation”.
“It doesn’t automatically transfer to commonwealth decisions or commonwealth legislation,” he told News24.
The NSW government was contacted for comment.

articles.title: Can I survive an action-packed day with the vivo V80 Lite – sans the power bank?
articles.summary: Let’s see how far its 10,000mAh battery can take us!

blocks.text: Let’s see how far its 10,000mAh battery can take us!

items: The vivo V80 Lite features a 10,000mAh Long-Lasting BlueVolt battery, allowing for two days of use on a single charge, making it ideal for busy individuals.

During extensive testing, the phone maintained impressive battery life and performance, even after heavy usage, and recently set a Guinness World Record for the longest electronic product live stream.

blocks.text: This is AI-generated. Read the article for full context. Report any errors.

Editor’s note: This content is sponsored by vivo and was produced by BrandRap, the sales and marketing arm of Rappler. No member of the news and editorial team participated in the production of this piece.
For a self-proclaimed “Type B” person, I can be a little obsessed with Plan Bs. This is why I love a reliable power bank.

I’m fine with carrying additional weight if it means having peace of mind, especially for someone like me who’s chronically busy (or doing too many side quests). Besides, I had previously used phones that would die on me midday, which would then require me to head to the nearest cafe and pray that they have an available electrical outlet.

Recently, I learned that vivo released a new smartphone in the roster, the vivo V80 Lite, which is specifically engineered for busybodies. Its core asset? The 10,000mAh Long-Lasting BlueVolt battery with 4th-Gen Silicon Anode technology. According to vivo, this device can let you go through two days with just a single charge. I wanted to try it myself for a whole weekend and one weekday with light to moderate use – mostly for taking photos and tinkering with a few of its apps – sans the power bank, of course.

For a phone that houses a massive battery capacity, it’s pretty slim to hold. I instantly got captivated by the Afterglow Pink variant, and was amazed at how the color scheme appeared so alive that I instantly likened it to a cotton candy sky. It sometimes looks like a painting, too, thanks to its “moonlight effect”. The texture is an experience in itself – it’s a mix of glossy, satin, and metallic, but not so delicate that you can feel it easily slipping from your hands, especially if you’re on the go.
It’s simply pretty that I didn’t have the urge to think of a good phone case to match it with – except the silicone case that’s included with the unit, for added protection.

blocks.caption: Using the different zooms of the vivo V80 Lite, which easily matches my outfit

blocks.text: Apart from good looks, the phone was also built to have military-grade durability, especially its resistance to foreign matter or unwanted liquid. Since the vivo V80 Lite is equipped with flagship-level IP68 & IP69 dust and water resistance (depending on your chosen variant), it felt easy to use even when it suddenly rained during one of my walks to finish an errand, and I was too preoccupied to fish out my umbrella.

There was also a moment when it got so sunny while I was waiting for my ride, but the performance didn’t change. The words on my screen were also still easy to read, thanks to the 1.5-high-brightness OLED display.

I went to a couple of places that varied in atmosphere: a heavily air-conditioned mall, a somewhat humid garden, and restaurants that, of course, contained a lot of steam and smoke in their cooking processes, among others. Apart from testing the quality of its body, it was a great way to test the 10,000mAh Long-Lasting BlueVolt battery – the largest battery capacity vivo has offered so far.

In total, I had a packed schedule during the three days of phone testing: a two-hour gift shopping session, my cousin’s birthday party, a spa appointment, a movie date with my mother, a coffee catch-up with my friends, an almost six-hour writing workshop, a walk in the park, and a lot of travelling from one spot to another, where I took a lot of photos.

Within this timeframe, I also streamed a two-hour movie and doomscrolled through shopping apps to watch livestreams. I also played classic games that were already ready to be downloaded on my vivo V80 Lite like Temple Run and Fruit Cut 3D. I was particularly impressed with the quality of my experience when I played League of Legends: Wild Rift, my favorite MLBB, as I didn’t experience any lag.

After the first day, my battery dropped to only 91%, after using the phone mostly for taking photos and watching videos. On the second day, I had more intensive use, from taking more photos to playing games, and I was left with 83% battery at the end of the day. On the third day, I was left with 61% after watching a movie, playing more games, and taking more photos.

No wonder. Proving its stellar battery life, the vivo V80 Lite recently set a Guinness World Records title, “The Longest Electronic Product Live Stream,” after completing a 32-hour and 37-minute continuous livestream in Thailand.

I’m not glued to my phone all the time, given my often hectic daily schedule. But that doesn’t mean I don’t need a durable and reliable one. After all, I mainly use my phone to document moments – big or small – because I enjoy chronicling my life as much as I enjoy actively participating in it.

While it’s easy to get lured in by over-the-top aesthetics and new complex features, I think it’s safe to say that we’ll always care about a gadget’s ability to keep up with our endurance. With the vivo V80 Lite, I feel powered up to take on the next action-packed day, even without the “peace” that comes with a power bank – or frankly, even just a charger.

Pre-order now until October 16 in vivo physical stores or online via the vivo e-store and vivo Store app. Enjoy up to a P1,500 discount, four-year battery warranty, Silver membership exclusive privileges, as well as free limited edition vivo Buds Air3 and 100GB of Google One cloud storage for six months.
Check out the full specs on vivo’s official website. The vivo V80 Lite starts at P24,999. – Rappler.com

articles.title: DOH monitoring reported 'plague' in Russia
articles.summary: Malacañang on Wednesday reassured the public that the Department of Health (DOH) is closely monitoring the reported plague in Russia.
articles.byline: JEAN MANGALUZ, JONATAHAN ANDAL, GMA News

blocks.text: PALACE SAYS
Published October 7, 2026 3:07pm
Malacañang on Wednesday reassured the public that the Department of Health (DOH) is closely monitoring the reported plague in Russia.
A laboratory worker in a Russian plague research institute died due to undisclosed circumstances earlier in October, sparking health concerns on social media.

"Nakausap po natin mismo ang DOH at closely monitoring po sila sa nagaganap lalong lalo na po at siniseryoso rin po ng DOH ang mga rekomendasyon ng WHO (World Health Organization) so rest assured po ang mga kababayan natin po na nakatutok po ang DOH at kung ano man po ang kinakailangan pang gawin, yun po ay kanilang gagawin,” Castro said in a press conference in Singapore.

(We have spoken to the DOH and they are closely monitoring, especially as the DOH is taking the WHO’s recommendations seriously so the public can rest assured that the DOH is focused on doing everything that needs to be done.)
EXPLAINER: What do we know about plague institute lab worker's death in Russia?
Castro said that the DOH has met all the requirements needed to curb the threat of the Russian plague.
"Baka kasi itong Russian plague ay isisi pa rin kay Pangulo Marcos Jr.,” Castro said.
(Because they might also blame this Russian plague on President Marcos Jr.)
While Castro did not disclose who would blame Marcos for the plague, she also addressed comments from several of Marcos’ critics during the same press conference.

Little is known so far about the Russian plague. After the laboratory worker’s death, around 200 people needed to be quarantined. Russian authorities said that the worker died of an unknown pneumonia.

Russia's health watchdog said on Tuesday that no cases of plague had been detected among anyone who had come into contact with a Siberian plague institute laboratory worker who died last week, and locals said their lives had barely been disrupted. —VAL, GMA News
