“I have a call scheduled, yes,” Trump told reporters at the White House when asked if he had spoken to Putin on the issue yet, adding that it would happen “very soon”.

Trump had said earlier that his administration was willing to offer assistance. “I hate to see them having it. We’ll help. Everybody who has that kind of a problem, we’ll always help,” he told reporters.
In an apparent mirror response, Rospotrebnadzor announced that Russia was prepared to assist the US in combating its own outbreaks of infectious diseases.

“The situation regarding dangerous infectious diseases remains unstable,” it said, highlighting a “significantly worsened” measles situation in three US states and a “fatal case of plague” recorded in New Mexico in June.
*With Agence France-Presse

articles.title: New Zealand greenhouse gas levels hit record highs threatening catastrophic glacier melts
articles.summary:
Government report finds the country could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves, as well as damaging storms and cyclones

New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense…

blocks.text: New Zealand could be hit with more frequent and intense heatwaves and catastrophic glacier melts in the near future, as greenhouse gas levels hit record highs, a new report about the nation’s climate has revealed.

Released on Wednesday, the Our Atmosphere and Climate 2026 report shows New Zealand is experiencing mounting climate pressures, which will have wide-reaching implications for the environment, native species and communities.

“The signal is just becoming clearer … there are multiple indicators that are showing increased warming and the likelihood of climate change,” Dr Alison Collins, chief science adviser for the ministry for cities, environment, regions and transport (Mcert) told the Guardian.
New Zealand’s annual average temperature has risen by 1.36C since records began in 1909, and seven of the 10 warmest years on record occurred in the last decade, the report said.
“Whilst it sounds like a small amount … it is a significant baseline shift that’s having ramifications through nature, through our communities, and through businesses and industry,” Collins said.

The report finds that as the climate heats, glaciers are shrinking. New Zealand has roughly 3000 glaciers, and they have shrunk in volume from 56 cubic kilometres in 1997 to 30 cubic kilometres in 2023, the report said.

Modelling of glacier retreat shows a high risk of further decline on the horizon. Under the “low climate scenario” – which assumes low emissions – glaciers will very likely lose between 14 and 86% of their volume by 2100. Under the “high climate scenario”, that figure rises to between 69 and 100% of their volume.
“We’re talking about substantial loss,” Collins said.

blocks.caption: Flooding caused by Cyclone Gabrielle in Awatoto, near the city of Napier.  Photograph: AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Greenhouse gases have increased to record levels in New Zealand’s atmosphere, the report shows. There was a 30% increase in carbon dioxide since monitoring began in New Zealand in 1972. Methane levels had also slightly increased in 2025 to their highest concentration ever.
“That additional heat is showing up in rising temperatures, warming oceans, rising seas, shifting rainfall patterns and more intense extremes,” the report said.

Among those extremes were heatwaves, which the report said were “very likely” to increase in frequency, length and intensity across the country. The number of days hitting more than 25C was also “very likely” to increase by 2050, which will expose people to heat-related health risks, including physical illness, disease and psychological distress.

Marine heatwaves are also becoming more pronounced and affecting some native species, the report said. In 2025, the series revealed New Zealand’s oceans were warming 34% faster than the global average which has been linked to mass sea sponge bleaching, die-offs of southern bull kelp, large scale fish standings and penguin deaths.

The three-yearly update from Mcert and Stats NZ collates statistics, data and research across five domains – air, atmosphere and climate, freshwater, land, and marine – to paint a picture of the state of New Zealand’s environment.

The report outlined a myriad of issues that will stem from continued warming, including damaging storms and cyclones that pose a risk to life, droughts affecting species and agricultural industries, sea level rise eroding infrastructure and housing and Māori communities having reduced access to culturally significant places.
Severe storms, including Cyclone Gabrielle and the Auckland floods in 2023, have battered New Zealand in recent years, causing deaths, widespread devastation and billions of dollars in costs.
New Zealand was built and developed around a relatively stable set of climate conditions and the report examines what happens when those conditions begin to change, Collins said.
“Climate change is not just an environmental issue. It’s a human story. It’s an economic story.”

articles.title: A beautiful Himalayan bird is changing its voice due to human activity, research shows
articles.summary: A sharp increase in human activity is affecting the way the Himalayan monal lives and communicates, studies show.

blocks.text: A sharp increase in human activity is having an impact on the way a Himalayan bird lives and communicates, two studies by Indian researchers have found.

The monal, a pheasant native to Himalayan mountain forests, is deeply woven into the region's cultural, folklore and identity. The eye-catching monal - the male has distinctive green, blue and copper feathers - is the state bird of India's Uttarakhand state and the national bird of Nepal, reflecting its cultural significance across the Himalayas.
But studies show that infrastructure development and tourism are squeezing its habitat, while increasing noise is altering how it communicates with potential mates and rivals.
Researchers from Uttarakhand conducted two separate studies over five years which flagged key threats to the bird.

One study found that the birds are forced to move higher in the mountains as their natural habitat in the alpine meadows above the tree line get crowded. The other says the monal is changing its pitch to cut through human noise in a busy valley.

"These two studies give a useful warning for other more vulnerable species - if the monal is forced to change both its voice and its address, how are the more sensitive species responding?" says Vishal Singh, an environmental practitioner working on ecology and climate issues in the Himalayas.

Dr Rajeev Lochan, lead researcher of both studies, told the BBC that they chose to study the monal as the bird has a narrow habitat range - it moves seasonally between the lower montane zone - an ecological belt found on the lower slopes of the mountains - and high-elevation alpine zones. This, he says, makes it a key indicator of ecosystem health in the north-western Himalayas.
"If the species is facing issues on this particular landscape, there might be a chance that the ecological disturbances are affecting other birds too," said Lochan.
The monal, researchers say, can be seen as a stand-in for the health of a fragile Himalayan ecosystem pushed to a tipping point due to unregulated tourism and heavy urbanisation.

While the region has always drawn tourists, trekkers and researchers given its scenic landscape and biodiversity, rapid infrastructure expansion in the past decade has made more places accessible, increasing footfall and disrupting the wildlife. This, coupled with mounting human pressures, suggests that climate change is emerging as another major threat to the region's already vulnerable biodiversity.
"There are a lot of factors at play but at a broader level, the problem is that the economic development of the region is not aligned to its ecological integrity," Singh said.

items: The Himalayas are melting faster - and India's economy is 'at risk'
Why the mighty Himalayas are getting harder and harder to see

blocks.text: According to the first study, climate change is projected to continue shrinking and destabilising the Himalayan monal's habitat across the Indian Himalayas through 2100 under multiple climate scenarios.
Currently, the birds are found in alpine meadows, located high in the mountains above the forests, which form some of the Himalayas' most important seasonal grazing and biodiversity-rich habitats.

The researchers modelled how climate change could shift the monal's suitable habitat across the Indian Himalayan region in the states of Uttarakhand and Himachal Pradesh. It was based on the kind of global climate models and emissions scenarios used for assessments by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC), the UN's climate science unit.

"These birds are now slowly moving upwards in the Himalayas as the snow is melting and vegetation is growing, making the area accessible to them. They are anyway being pushed upwards as their natural habitats in alpine meadows are being encroached upon by humans," Lochan said.
The model assumes that the bird needs the current climate set-up that exists in alpine meadows in the future too, a reasonable but not certain assumption.

The birds' seasonal migration may become increasingly difficult as changes in climate may force them to move to higher elevations on hills, to smaller and fragmented areas. Their population would be scattered in disconnected pockets, which reduces chances of breeding between groups and increases their risks of long-term decline or local extinction, which is already a threat, the study says.

The second study, also conducted by Lochan, Dinesh Kumar Sharma and Anand Kumar, who work at the Hemvati Nandan Bahuguna Garhwal University, focuses on the bird's behavioural changes. They conducted the study in two valleys in Kedarnath Musk Deer Sanctuary in Uttarakhand - at Chopta, a tourist spot with busy traffic and visitors, and the largely quiet Madmaheshwar.
They recorded more than 700 monal calls across both sites using microphones and passive recording devices and then measured pitch, call length and background noise levels for a year from April 2023.
Birds in noisy environments consistently produced calls with significantly higher peak frequencies compared with those in quieter habitats, the study said.
The researchers found subtle changes in the monal's pitch that could be picked up by recording devices but might go unnoticed by the human ear.

"This does not mean that the species has undergone a permanent or evolutionary change in its vocal frequency; rather, our findings suggest behavioural flexibility in response to different acoustic environments," Lochan said.
Compared with the birds in Madmaheshwar valley, the monal in Chopta also produced shorter call durations likely to cut through low-frequency human noise from traffic and tourist footfall.
Bird calls are one of the most sophisticated forms of sound-based communication in the natural world, and significant changes can interfere with, among other things, their mating success.

"When a species must raise its pitch to be heard over tourist traffic, or climb higher as meadows turn crowded, it reveals how human pressure is rewriting the rules of life in the Himalaya," says Anjal Prakash, a public policy professor at FLAME University and contributor to IPCC reports.
Lochan says he and his team consider this a preliminary study and hope to expand the scope and depth of it.

The research comes with the caveat that it is not conclusive on ecological consequences, and more research is needed. But together, the two studies signal broader ecological stress across the Himalayas.
"In listening to the monal, we hear the Himalayas asking for space, silence and care," says Prakash.

articles.title: Eva Marie Saint, Oscar-winning On the Waterfront actor, dead at 102
articles.summary: Eva Marie Saint, the pale, willowy actor who won an Academy Award for her first movie, On the Waterfront, and starred opposite Cary Grant in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller North by Northwest, has…

image.caption: U.S. actor Eva Marie Saint, in the U.K. in 1966. Saint, the pale, willowy actor who won an Academy Award for her first movie, On the Waterfront, and starred opposite Cary Grant in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller North by Northwest, has died. She was 102. (Evening Standard/Hulton Archive/Getty Images)

blocks.text: Entertainment·New

Eva Marie Saint, the pale, willowy actor who won an Academy Award for her first movie, On the Waterfront, and starred opposite Cary Grant in the Alfred Hitchcock thriller North by Northwest, has died. She was 102.
Hollywood star also featured opposite Cary Grant in North by Northwest
Saint, whose acting work lasted well into her 90s, died at her home in Los Angeles on Tuesday, confirmed family representative Jeff Sanderson.

Saint had one of the most spectacular debuts in Hollywood history as the love interest of Marlon Brando's tormented Terry Malloy in On the Waterfront, and her first trip to the Academy Awards was memorable, too. Pregnant with her first child, Saint accepted her Oscar from Frank Sinatra and smilingly murmured a unique winner's speech: "I think I may have the baby right here." (Her son, Darrell, was born two days later.)

The award for the 1954 classic made her an instant star, but she soon astonished Hollywood with a firm independence that would mark her career. She refused offers of studio contracts and declined chances to follow up on her great success, explaining that she was taking time off to become acquainted with her new son. (A daughter, Laurette, was born in 1958.)

In her first decade in Hollywood, Saint appeared in a mere seven films. She declined such top-level productions as The Man in the Gray Flannel Suit with Gregory Peck, Summer and Smoke with Laurence Harvey and The Rainmaker with Burt Lancaster. She credited her husband, TV and stage director Jeffrey Hayden, with persuading her to star in Hitchcock's North by Northwest, the classic 1959 thriller in which Saint plays a spy who seduces Grant's character, but ends up falling for him.
In her first decade in Hollywood, Saint appeared in a mere seven films. (Keystone Features/Getty Images)

"I vividly remember him saying, 'Honey, I think you should find a quiet spot. I'll take care of the children and I want you to really think about this and reread this script,"' she told Vanity Fair in 2014. "He was so right. And that's what husbands are for."

Instead of being put off by her selectivity, studios continued offering her starring roles in such films as Exodus (with Newman), Raintree County (with Elizabeth Taylor and Montgomery Clift) and All Fall Down, with Warren Beatty.

items: Jeffrey Hayden, veteran TV & stage director, dead at 90

blocks.text: She turned more to television in the 1970s and enjoyed renewed popularity in the 1980s as the mother of Cybill Shepherd in the hit sitcom Moonlighting and as Tom Hanks's mother in the comedy film Nothing in Common. She won an Emmy for the 1990 miniseries People Like Us, and had roles in such 21st-century movies as Because of Winn-Dixie, Superman Returns and Winter's Tale, the latter of which was adapted from Mark Helprin's novel of the same name. In 2021, she played Marisa Tomei's aunt in the brief audio play The Bus Ride, part of The Pack Podcast.
Saint was married to Hayden for 55 years, until his death in 2016.
Saint, left, and husband, Jeffrey Hayden, attend an event in Los Angeles in October 1957. Saint was married to Hayden for 55 years, until his death in 2016. (Harold P. Matosian/The Associated Press)

When Saint emerged in the public consciousness, many believed her theatrical-sounding name must have been invented. She was born with it on July 4, 1924, in Newark, N.J. The family moved to Delmar, a small town near Albany, N.Y., where her father was a Goodrich Rubber Co. manager. Saint's goal was to become a third-grade teacher like her mother, but at Bowling Green State University in Ohio she tried out for a play and won the leading role.

After graduation she lived with her parents in Flushing, Long Island, and began hunting for acting jobs in Manhattan. After a fruitless year, she landed a two-line role as a telephone operator on a radio drama and soon was working steadily on soap operas and nighttime dramas, appearing for two years as Claudia on One Man's Family. Network television was booming in the early 1950s, and her looks and dramatic sense made her a favourite with casting people and producers.

A critical turn in Saint's career came when she auditioned before Elia Kazan and was accepted into the Actors Studio, which shaped a generation of method-actor stars. She credited acting coach Lee Strasberg with helping her overcome her shyness.
PHOTOS | Eva Marie Saint and some of her roles:

"Lee Strasberg, when he got to know me a little bit, gave me a scene to do where I had to cry in front of my peers," she told the Santa Barbara Independent in 2009. "I worried about it, I worked on it, I tried to use what I was learning at the studio. I finally did the scene, and I cried, and my peers were crying with me. It was just an incredible moment for me."

Saint was rejected for the single female role in the play Mister Roberts, but was hired to understudy the actor chosen, Jocelyn Brando, Marlon's sister. In six frustrating months, Saint never got to substitute for Brando. She finally made it to Broadway in A Trip to Bountiful, which she had played on television.

Kazan invited her to try out for the female lead in On the Waterfront by improvising a scene with Marlon Brando. She was told to try to stop a young man from entering her apartment. She told the Los Angeles Times in 2001: "All I know is that Marlon got in the door and turned on the music. We started dancing. He flicked my skirt. Kazan saw the sparks fly, and that's how I got the part."

articles.title: Ikea to pilot online buyback service for secondhand furniture
articles.summary:
Service to be tested in Spain and Portugal this year, with a UK rollout if successful, as pre-loved markets boom

Ikea is to test an…

blocks.text: Ikea is to test an online version of its buy-back service where the retailer offers vouchers for unwanted secondhand furniture.

The service will be tested in Spain and Portugal before the end of December and will be launched in the UK if it proves successful. Ikea already offers buy-back in stores, including in the UK. The online version will extend it to a much wider audience, with Ikea predicting pre-owned goods are likely to grab 16% of the UK homewares market by next year
The new plan emerged as the world’s largest furniture retailer takes on Vinted and eBay with its own secondhand online marketplace which launches in the UK this week.

The platform, which is already online in other countries including Spain and Portugal with bestsellers including the Kallax shelving system and Malm chest of drawers, will enable shoppers signed up to the Swedish company’s membership scheme to connect directly to one another to buy and sell pre-owned Ikea items locally.

The UK service will be free initially, but a “buyer protection fee” of about 5% of an item’s price will be introduced in time. At launch, buyers and sellers will arrange collection or delivery directly with one another through the marketplace. Ikea said it is exploring ways to make delivery easier in future.

“The secondhand market is growing and growing. It is now really significant,” said Greg Lucas, sustainability manager at Ikea’s UK & Irish division. “Secondhand browsing and shopping is now mainstream.

“The way people furnish their homes has changed. Whether they are moving, redecorating or looking for a particular piece, more customers are considering pre-owned furniture alongside new and are actively searching for items that can help create a home that feels personal to them.”

The secondhand home products market is now worth more than £4.5bn in the UK and is growing at about 6.5% annually. Ikea said its products accounted for about 9% of furniture sold on secondhand marketplaces in the UK.

Ikea said it was making the sale of used versions of its products easier by providing pre-filled product descriptions and price suggestions. The company also offers sellers 15% extra on the price of the item sold if they agree to be paid in the form of an Ikea gift card.
The change is part of a revolution in retail, where shoppers of all ages are now prepared to consider secondhand items.
In 2025, 63% of UK consumers bought products through reselling platforms, up from 51% in 2024.
after newsletter promotion

The trend has boosted sales at Vinted, which began as a clothing resale site but is now expanding into homewares and electronics, as well as at Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree and smaller, more upmarket sites such as Vinterior.
The US secondhand site eBay recently bought UK fashion seller Depop for $1.2bn (£900m). Preloved items now make up about a 10th of global fashion sales.
There is heavy competition for the secondhand market, with the electrical goods retailers Currys and AO, for example, both selling pre-owned items.

AO expanded its secondhand position after acquiring MusicMagpie, which sells refurbished electronics and secondhand video games, in 2024. It recently also bought camera specialist Jessops, which controls the Camera Jungle secondhand site.

articles.title: LA and San Diego residents ‘horrified’ by Trump’s comment: ‘obsessed with us’
articles.summary:
As Angelenos bemoan ‘sad situation’, those in San Diego say remark a ‘disservice’ to town with multiple naval bases

Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los…
articles.byline: Roque Planas and Sam Levin in Los Angeles

blocks.text: Donald Trump’s extraordinary implication that Iran could “take out” Los Angeles and San Diego have sparked condemnation across the political spectrum. As residents of the two major west coast cities awoke on Tuesday to another sweltering day in a record-breaking heatwave, the president’s comments sent blood boiling even higher.
Jessica, a 28-year-old Los Angeles hair stylist, was scrolling through social media early on Tuesday morning and was shocked to see that Trump had just suggested Iran should decimate her home town.

For Jessica, who declined to be identified by her full name because she fears for the safety of her Mexican-born parents, the comments marked a new low for a president who had already spent years attacking immigrant families like hers.

“I was just thinking what the fuck is wrong with him?” she said while waiting for a Waymo outside grocery store in LA’s Koreatown neighborhood. “He hates us. He hates LA. He hates any Democratic state ... It’s just a really sad situation.”

In southern California, Trump’s unprecedented musing before a cheering crowd at a Nebraska rally on Monday night – that perhaps a foreign power should decimate two of the country’s best-known cities – has been met with reactions ranging from deep hostility to dismissive incredulity. Gavin Newsom, the state’s governor, called the remarks “dangerous – if not treasonous – putting a target on two of our biggest cities and one of America’s largest naval hubs”.

Perhaps most of all, California residents see it as a sign of the president’s fixation on tearing down west coast progressivism and diversity, most visibly through the deployment of national guard troops in Los Angeles during a series of brutal ICE raids in 2025.

During a bustling lunch service at Grand Central Market, a food hall in downtown LA, tourists and residents milled between taco stands and dumpling stalls. Many had yet to hear of the president’s threats, until asked by a reporter. One of those who had was Jens Midthun, a downtown resident who often stops at the market for coffee.

blocks.caption: Trump suggested Iran could ‘take out’ LA and San Diego at a rally. Photograph: Harry How/Getty Images

blocks.text: “Trump has tried to paint Los Angeles as a dystopia despite it being a wonderful place,” said Midthun, sipping an iced coffee under a shaded outdoor table as the temperature approached the triple digits. (Midthun serves as the president of the downtown LA neighborhood council, but was speaking only on behalf of himself.)

“It reminded me that the president is obsessed with us – obsessed with California, obsessed with Los Angeles,” Midthun said. “We try not to think about him and yet, here he is with Los Angeles’s name right there in his mouth.”

Trump’s remarks have sparked a particularly strong reaction in San Diego, which is home to roughly a quarter-million veterans and has one of the largest concentrations of military personnel in the US.

“His statement was so irrational, it’s hard to explain exactly what he was saying, but it sounded like he was willing to give us up,” said Gil Field, communications director for San Diego Veterans for Peace, a group that opposes the war. “It’s horrible and we’re horrified.”

The military supports nearly 357,000 local jobs in the region, representing $61.3bn of San Diego county’s economy, according to a report released last year. Defense spending accounts for 22% of San Diego’s gross regional product and the area is home to multiple naval bases and Marine Corps stations, with one out of four active-duty marines based in San Diego.

“This is a military town, so you’ve got bipartisan objections to his comments,” said Field, who noted that there were always concerns that San Diego could be targeted in war due to the heavy military presence. “So for him to say this about San Diego is particularly galling. He did San Diego a disservice.”
Jim Desmond, a Republican naval veteran running for a congressional seat in San Diego, also offered a pointed rebuke.

blocks.caption: Navy ships are lined at the Naval Base San Diego.  Photograph: The San Diego Union-Tribune/Getty Images

blocks.text: “I served to protect Americans, not write off American cities as an acceptable price of war. Our job is to keep Americans safe, stand up to our enemies, and make sure a threat like that never becomes reality,” Desmond said on X. “No American city is expendable, and no American family should ever be treated as collateral damage.”

Back in Los Angeles, far from the negative fantasies that Trump spins in his speeches, Midthun sees an economic powerhouse and vibrant cultural center sandwiched between the beach and the mountains, and enriched by some of the largest diaspora communities from across the world – South Korea, Mexico, El Salvador, Armenia and even Iran.

“The president keeps talking about us, and talking about us,” Midthun said. “He’s got a lot of issues to solve. He should work on those issues instead of obsessing over the beautiful, great people of Los Angeles.”

articles.title: Many Nepalis swept away in the floods aren't officially dead, leaving families in limbo
articles.summary: Relatives are finding themselves with no compensation and facing an administrative nightmare.

blocks.text: Image source, AFP via Getty Images
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead
ByAzadeh Moshiri
South Asia correspondent

At the Pashupatinath temple, on the banks of the Bagmati River in Kathmandu, Madan Lal Lawat joined other families in honouring loved ones who were lost when a deadly flood tore through the China-Nepal border last month.
In Hindu tradition, when a body cannot be recovered, a symbolic effigy is made from sacred "kusha" grass to represent the dead, allowing relatives to perform last rites.
With more than 5,000 people still missing and the government ending rescue operations, this is the only way people like Lawat can honour the dead.
Five of his relatives - including his brother - were caught in the water's onslaught and are still missing. Lawat survived because he was driving his bus outside his village, Betrawati.
The last Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave.
"I don't know how to start over. Police say they're still searching for the bodies, but I'm not sure they'll ever be found," Lawat says.
He has little doubt they are dead.
But legally, their fate is far more complicated. In Nepal, a missing person is only presumed dead after 12 years.

blocks.caption: Image caption, The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave

blocks.text: Image source, Supplied
The last Madan Lal Lawat heard from survivors is that his brother Mangal (pictured) died while going door-to-door, trying to warn others to leave
Section 40 of Nepal's Civil Code does allow for some exceptions, but it does not have a provision for disasters like the flood witnessed last month.
Families like Lawat's have told the BBC they are struggling to obtain death certificates, affecting everything from accessing flood compensation to the transfer of properties and even inheritance.

Relatives can receive up to 25,000 rupees (£122; $162) for funeral costs, in addition to about 200,000 rupees (£981; $1,302) in bereavement compensation for the first relative who died, and 100,000 rupees (£491; $651) for each additional death.
But this is only possible once they submit a death certificate. So as families try to rebuild their lives, many are now caught in an administrative nightmare.
"In view of the current disaster, the law is outdated," says constitutional law expert, Bipin Adhikari.

He explains the law was meant to account for people who travelled abroad and weren't heard from for years. "But technology has advanced now, it isn't as difficult to send or receive information," he argues.
For Lawat, the legal minefield has made an already devastating loss even harder to navigate.

When he tried to obtain a death certificate last week, officials at the local municipality office turned him away. "They said they're still discussing the death certificate issue. We aren't sure what to do now. There's so much uncertainty," he tells us.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods

blocks.text: Most of Betrawati village was swallowed up in the floods

Even when bodies are recovered, identifying their identities is a slow and challenging task. More than 1,400 bodies have been recovered so far, and Nepal has little experience in processing DNA at such scale. In some cases, authorities have taken DNA samples, then buried the bodies with markers in the ground, should families claim them.
Given the scale of damage and loss, families say compensation is desperately needed.
Nepal's latest assessment counts 7,570 private buildings damaged or destroyed, home to nearly 33,000 people based on census data.

The BBC visited Lawat's village Betrawati just days after the disaster, once the roads to the district of Rasuwa had been cleared. For days, this area had been cut off from the capital Kathmandu, and struggling with a shortage of basic supplies including petrol.

The damage in the village was staggering. The ground was nothing but hardened mud and silt. Footage of the flood showed it had swallowed most of the village in just minutes. There was no sign of its bustling market, the local Uttargaya School was in ruins, the houses swept away, and school buses were turned over.

Betrawati straddles flood-devastated Rasuwa and Nuwakot, and is part of the Bidur municipality, where the government estimates more than 3,000 buildings have been damaged or destroyed. It's the largest amount of any municipality.
Local governments are now urging the prime minister's office to figure out a way to resolve the death confirmation issue.
"Everything is on hold," Bidur's Mayor, Rajan Shrestha, told the BBC.
He said it could take up to 12 years for relatives to access the funds they are entitled to.
For one of South Asia's smallest economies, finding money for compensation is a challenge, and the sums on offer are small when compared with the scale of the losses.

blocks.caption: Image caption, More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief

blocks.text: More than 5,000 people are still missing after the floods, leaving families stricken with grief
The government puts damage to personal belongings alone at £123 million ($165 million) across more than 8,300 households.
This implies losses of about £14,800 ($20,000) on average per household, though this figure is only based on census data and modelling, and doesn't represent the exact cost per family.
The financial toll makes the death certificates vital for families trying to recover from the disaster.
Shrestha is calling on the federal government to resolve the issue as soon as possible. Until then, he says his hands are tied.
"We understand the emotional pain for families who have already performed funeral rituals, but officials must work within legal boundaries to avoid future liabilities."
The government has told the BBC it is trying to find a solution.

In a statement, the prime minister's office said it was "aware of the difficulties" the law may cause families in "exceptional circumstances, including disasters". The home ministry said the government was taking the issue seriously and was ready to amend the law, if required.
The legal hurdles families are facing comes as Nepal faces a steep reconstruction bill, which the government says could cost up to £3.6bn ($4.8bn).

blocks.caption: Image caption, Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing

blocks.text: Image source, Getty Images
Relatives carry Kush grass effigies for cremation during symbolic funerals held for flood victims still reported missing

At the UN General Assembly in New York, Prime Minister Balen Shah explained rebuilding the country would require more than 10% of its gross domestic product, an enormous burden on the country's economy.
Dozens of public buildings including schools, health clinics and hospitals have been wrecked by the floods. That's in addition to roads, bridges, wastewater treatment plants and hydropower projects.

Shah is now pushing for grant-based international support rather than new loans. Nepal is one of the lowest emitters of global greenhouse gas emissions, yet one one of the most vulnerable countries to global warming.
"When a climate-driven disaster destroys infrastructure of a poor country, the answer cannot simply be another mega-loan or a patchwork of small grants," he told a room full of world leaders.
This is not the first time Nepal has had to recover after a devastating natural disaster.
For Tisum Ghale, the past month has been painfully familiar.
He and his family lost their home in an earthquake in 2015, and became displaced for months. They eventually settled in Betrawati.

But the place that was once a refuge is where 19 of his relatives were killed in last month's flood, including five of his sisters. He survived because he was doing construction work outside of the village.
Once again, he is without a home.
"I have lost everything," he said.

So far he has received no compensation. He desperately needs the money after his home was washed away and he looks after eight children left behind by his sisters. He is one of the thousands displaced, living across 37 holding centres in northern Nepal.
Like Lawati and thousands of other families, Ghale plans on holding a funeral without his loved ones' bodies.
He hopes the law will eventually recognise what he already knows: his loved ones will not be coming home.
Additional reporting: Rajneesh Bhandari

articles.title: US man arrested as second suspect in Canada mass school shooting planned with ChatGPT
articles.summary:
Justice department detained James Codey Bryant and allege he offered ‘technical advice’ to primary suspect

A surprise suspected accomplice has been arrested in connection with a mass school…

blocks.text: A surprise suspected accomplice has been arrested in connection with a mass school shooting in Canada that was made notorious after an 18-year-old allegedly killed six children after discussing it with the AI chatbot ChatGPT.
The US Department of Justice said Tuesday it had detained James Codey Bryant, 30, a resident of western Washington state, on a charge of conspiracy to murder persons in a foreign country.
Bryant offered money and “technical advice” to the suspected shooter for six months leading up to the killings, the justice department alleged.

Canadian police have identified the suspect in this year’s massacre of eight people – including her mother and half-brother, as well as the six children, making it the second-deadliest school shooting in the country’s history – as Jesse Van Rootselaar, who has a history of mental health problems.

It had been known that Van Rootselaar had used ChatGPT to plan the attack, which took place in February. The safety team at OpenAI, the company that owns the chatbot, flagged Van Rootselaar internally after she conducted conversations with it about gun violence, but the company did not alert police. It did reportedly close Van Rootselaar’s account, but she started a second one that was not closed. Victims’ families and the province of British Columbia have sued OpenAI and its CEO, Sam Altman, for failing to report her behaviour.
It was not previously known publicly that Van Rootselaar was also talking to a human about her plans.

In a joint press conference with the justice department and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) on Tuesday, authorities alleged that Bryant and Van Rootselaar met on the now-defunct messaging service Omegle about three years prior to the shooting and kept in contact.

Neil Floyd, acting US attorney, and W Mike Herrington, the special agent in charge for the FBI’s Seattle bureau, said they believe Bryant sent Van Rootselaar about $100 to buy new shoes and aabout $15 for a lighter.
Authorities said there is no indication so far that the two suspects ever met in person.
According to an indictment obtained by CBC, Bryant was “knowingly and wilfully” conspiring with Van Rootselaar beginning in or before August 2025.

That August, Bryant told Van Rootselaar the pair should “find a way to delete” their messages, and in mid-December Bryant suggested getting a VPN to avoid detection for “posting a shooting video online”, according to the court document reviewed by CBC.
Police said that on several occasions Bryant tried to talk Van Rootselaar out of committing the attack, but did not contact law enforcement.

They added that after Van Rootselaar shot and killed her mother and brother in their family home, she was unable to start the car. Bryant advised her on how to turn on the engine, thereby allowing the shooter to reach the school and execute the attack, authorities said.
Bryant also allegedly agreed to livestream the mass shooting, which Harrington said police were not sure Van Rootselaar would have committed had Bryant not done so.

It was not clear whether the suspect was represented by a lawyer. Bryant will be prosecuted in the US as a US citizen under an investigation by the FBI, which said it will continue working closely with Canadian authorities.

articles.title: Fruit of the Loom, Hanes investigated over potential toxic chemicals in children's underwear
articles.summary: Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton launched an investigation on Tuesday into whether Fruit of the Loom and Hanes use toxic chemicals in producing ‌children's underwear.

image.caption: Packages of Hanes underwear. The Texas attorney general launched an investigation on Tuesday into whether Fruit of the Loom and Hanes use toxic chemicals in producing ‌children's underwear. (Chuck Burton/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: Health·New
Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton launched an investigation on Tuesday into whether Fruit of the Loom and Hanes use toxic chemicals in producing ‌children's underwear.
Canadian company Gildan Activewear owns Hanes, says it will co-operate with investigation
· Thomson Reuters
· Posted: Oct 06, 2026 5:58 PM EDT | Last Updated: 2 minutes ago

Paxton said he sent civil investigative demands to Fruit of the Loom, which is owned by Berkshire Hathaway, and Hanes, which is owned by Canadian company Gildan Activewear, citing the chemicals' ​potential effects on children's health.
He did ​not accuse either company of wrongdoing.
Fruit of the Loom and Berkshire did not immediately respond to requests from Reuters for comment.
Montreal-based Gildan ​said it will co-operate with the investigation, and maintains ⁠strict manufacturing and ⁠sourcing standards to comply with ‌industry guidelines related to harmful chemicals.
"We remain committed to providing safe, high-quality products for consumers," it said in a statement to Reuters.
Gildan merged with Massachusetts-based HanesBrands Inc. last year in a $2.2-billion US deal.
Paxton said clothing manufacturers have turned increasingly to synthetic materials such as polyester, rayon and ⁠spandex to meet consumer demand for lower-priced products.

He said research shows that synthetic fabrics can shed microplastics, while chemicals including bisphenols, fluorine, parabens, phthalates and ‌so-called "forever chemicals" used in textile manufacturing have been associated with cancer, hormone disruption, infertility and other health concerns.
"Forever chemicals" are also known as PFAS, ​short for per- ⁠and polyfluoroalkyl substances.

items: Texas attorney general launches investigation into Lululemon's potential use of certain chemicals
New bans target PFAS in clothing. Here's how to avoid exposure (2025)

blocks.text: "We must protect our children who cannot yet protect themselves," Paxton said in a ​news release.
"This includes making sure that the necessities parents rely on are free from toxic chemicals ⁠and do not harm the health of kids."
The attorney general ⁠announced a similar probe in April into whether Vancouver-based Lululemon Athletica activewear ⁠contained "forever ⁠chemicals," which do not ​break down easily in nature.
Paxton, a Republican, is running for a U.S. Senate seat against Democrat James Talarico and trailing in most polls.
The race is among the country's most closely watched in the Nov. 3 midterm elections.
Canada to add most ‘forever chemicals’ to toxic substances list

articles.title: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike awake and speaking after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.summary: Christa Pike, a Tennessee inmate who survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday.

image.caption: Tennessee inmate Christa Pike is seen in a file photo taken Dec. 4, 2007. Pike, a Tennessee inmate who recently survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday. (J. Miles Cary/Knoxville News Sentinel/Reuters)

blocks.text: World·Updated
Christa Pike, a Tennessee inmate who survived Tennessee's attempt to execute her, is awake and speaking as she receives treatment at a hospital, her attorneys said Tuesday.
Survived 2 doses of pentobarbital
Pike's attorneys said her prognosis is still "unclear" and said she faces "a long recovery."

"Against all odds, Christa Pike is conscious, speaking, and continues to receive critical medical care," attorneys for Pike said in a statement. "Despite the severe damage she endured to her arms, she is still handcuffed and shackled to the bed. Her recovery is medically unprecedented."
Her lawyers said they are grateful for the first responders and the medical team at the hospital "who treated Christa like a human and have provided exceptional care to her."
The statement was the first indication that Pike has improved since an ambulance carried her away from a Nashville prison last Wednesday.
Pike's arms left burned, blistered

Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital as they attempted to put her to death for the 1995 beating and stabbing death of classmate Colleen Slemmer. The lethal injection drug didn't kill her, but her lawyers said her arms were left burned and blistered.
As recently as Sunday, her attorneys said Pike had remained unconscious and on a ventilator since the failed execution attempt.

Dr. Joel Zivot, a professor of anesthesiology and surgery in Atlanta who consulted as an expert for Pike's legal team, said the development "bodes well for a good recovery." But he added that it could be weeks or months before anyone knows exactly what her recovery might look like or whether her competency could be restored to a level that might enable the state to try to execute her again.

"She's still in the ICU," he said. "She has recovered to a certain degree that she's able to be off a ventilator and able to speak, but in no way would I announce her free of further serious risk. There's still a lot of bad things that can happen here, even when everyone is doing their job well."

items: Tennessee prisons chief to resign after failed execution of Christa Pike, governor says
Christa Pike on ventilator after surviving Tennessee execution attempt, lawyer says

blocks.text: A spokesperson for the Tennessee Department of Correction said she could provide no information other than that Pike remained hospitalized Tuesday.
Pike's attorneys are set to go to court Wednesday as they seek to learn more about what happened in the failed lethal injection.

The attorneys are seeking a court order requiring the Tennessee Department of Correction to preserve evidence, including drug lot numbers, records and other information from the Sept. 30 attempted execution. Chancery Court Judge I'Ashea Myles scheduled a Wednesday morning status conference in the case.
Pike's attorneys said in their Tuesday statement that they continue to ask Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee to commute Pike's sentence to life in prison without the possibility of parole.
"Christa is a survivor and will take recovery one day at a time," her attorneys said.

articles.title: Watch: Riot police clash with school protesters and use tear gas in France
articles.summary: Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France amid a wave of protests by high-school pupils.

blocks.text: Hundreds of thousands of people have taken to the streets across France, as a wave of protests by high-school pupils spread to their parents, university students and unions.
Crowds of teenagers marched from the Place de la République in Paris, calling for more resources for schools, and what they called less repression from police.
Police clashed with demonstrators in Lyon, used tear gas in Paris and Marseille and water cannon in Rennes, but there was little of the serious trouble that marred previous protests.
The BBC's Europe correspondent Nick Beake reports from Lille.

articles.title: US death row inmate Christa Pike conscious after failed execution, lawyers say
articles.summary: Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, according to a statement from her lawyers on Tuesday.

blocks.text: US death row inmate Christa Pike is "conscious and speaking" after her failed execution attempt, her lawyers say.
Pike, 50, continues to receive critical medical care while handcuffed in hospital, according to a statement from her attorneys on Tuesday.

She was sentenced to death following her conviction for murdering Colleen Slemmer in 1995. But Pike survived two lethal injections last week and was transferred to a hospital in Nashville, Tennessee, for treatment.
Her lawyers had said in the days afterwards that she was unconscious while medical staff cleared her body of the pentobarbitol injected during the failed execution attempt.
Pike's lawyers said on Tuesday that her recovery is "medically unprecedented", and while her prognosis remains unclear, "at a minimum, we expect a long recovery".
They said she is the only person known to have survived a completed execution attempt in the US.
Authorities have not yet said whether they will try again to execute Pike. They have also not offered an explanation for what went wrong.
Tennessee Governor Bill Lee suspended all executions for the rest of the year - and the head of prisons in the state said over the weekend that he plans to resign.
Pike was 18 when she and her then-boyfriend, Tadaryl Shipp, beat, tortured and killed 19-year-old Slemmer, whom they had met at a job training camp for troubled teens.

articles.title: Outrage in Japan after U.S. Marine accused of murdering Okinawan woman
articles.summary: A U.S. Marine was arrested this week on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman in Okinawa. The killing has drawn outrage on the island and inflamed longstanding tensions over U.S. military…

image.caption: Protesters, many of them Okinawan women, outside the U.S. Embassy in Tokyo on Wednesday after a U.S. Marine was arrested on suspicion of murder. (Christopher Jue/AFP/Getty Images)

blocks.text: As It Happens·New

A U.S. Marine was arrested this week on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman in Okinawa. The killing has drawn outrage on the island and inflamed longstanding tensions over U.S. military bases, which residents say are a source of noise, pollution and violent crime against women.
History of violence by U.S. soldiers against women and girls goes back decades
All her life, 24-year-old Sorane Sakihama has heard stories about crimes committed against Japanese women by U.S. soldiers stationed in Okinawa, Japan.
So when a U.S. Marine was arrested this week on suspicion of robbing and killing a local woman at a hotel in the island's capital city of Naha, Sakihama decided she had to do something.
"As an Okinawan, I don't want to see any victims again," she told As It Happens host Nil Köksal. "We have to end this history."
Sakihama helped organize a protest outside the U.S. embassy in Tokyo on Tuesday, where hundreds of people came to demand justice and call for the ouster of U.S. military bases from Okinawa.
It was one of several protests across the country this week.
About 160 people gathered at a protest Sunday in Naha, demanding U.S. bases be removed from the island.
One sign read: "We've had enough of this!"
LISTEN | Interview with protest organizer Sorane Sakihama:
As It Happens6:19Japanese protesters take to the streets after U.S. Marine accused of murdering Okinawan woman

Okinawa police have arrested Lance Cpl. Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, who is stationed at Futenma Air Station, on suspicion of strangling Anna Yagi, 39, on Saturday and stealing her wallet and backpack. Ballard denied the allegations, ​police said.
Sakihama, who grew up in the town of Chatan, didn't know Yagi personally, but says she has met people who did.
"People say she's a really good, kind person."
Devin Jacob Ballard, a U.S. Marine, has been arrested on suspicion of robbing and murdering Anna Yagi, 39. Police say he denies the allegations. (Kotaro Ueda/Kyodo News/The Associated Press)
The killing has drawn outrage in Okinawa and inflamed longstanding tensions over the military bases, which many locals see as a source of noise, pollution and violent crime.
Okinawa was under U.S. occupation from the Second World War until 1972. Today, it is home to 70 per cent of the U.S. military facilities based in Japan, and hosts 18,000 U.S. Marines.
"My grandparents experienced World War II, and what they say is that the military never protected us," Sakihama said.
"They really wanted to have their own land back, but they couldn't."
Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi called the killing "an extremely brutal and vicious incident" and called on the U.S. to co-operate with the police investigation.
History of violence against women and girls

The number of U.S. military-related criminal cases on Okinawa rose to 101 last year from about 40 in 2020, according to local police. But the history of violence by U.S. soldiers against women and girls goes back much further.
In 1995, the rape of a 12-year-old ​Okinawan girl by three U.S. servicemen sparked mass protests. In 2013, two U.S. sailors pleaded guilty to the rape of a Japanese woman in Okinawa.
In 2016, a worker on a U.S. air force base admitted to strangling Rina Shimabukuro, a 20-year-old woman whose body was found in undergrowth.
In 2024, a U.S. Air Force member was charged with kidnapping and raping a teenager girl in Okinawa, and was later sentenced to five years in prison.
"Nothing has changed," Sakihama said. "[As long as] we have bases in Okinawa, the situation won't change."
Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja, left, speaks to the media in Naha, Okinawa, on Sunday, calling the murder of a local woman 'absolutely unforgivable.' (Kyodo News/The Asscociated Press)
Okinawa Gov. Genta Koja said this latest murder underscores the ineffectiveness of past disciplinary measures taken by the U.S. military following similar crimes.

"The case deals a major shock and adds fear to the Okinawans who have already been forced to live next to U.S. bases," Koja told reporters Sunday night in Naha. "It is absolutely unforgivable and we are outraged."
The U.S. embassy and the Marine ⁠Corps expressed condolences over Yagi's murder and said they were co-operating with the Japanese authorities.
"The Marine Corps takes these allegations very seriously and expects every Marine to adhere to the highest standards of behaviour," it ​said in a written statement.
George Glass, the U.S. ambassador to Japan, wrote on X that he spoke to U.S. military about holding "our American service members to the very highest levels of discipline and integrity."
What happens next?
Despite strongly worded statements from Japanese and U.S. officials, Sakihama says she doesn't believe they will remove the U.S. military presence from Okinawa.
"I don't expect anything from them," she said.

Prime Minister Takaichi has been pushing to strengthen Japanese military presence and collaborate with U.S. officers on island, which is viewed by Tokyo and Washington as key in deterring ⁠potential military aggression from ‌China.
A woman holds a sign demanding the closure of U.S. military bases in Japan during a protest outside the Japanese prime minister's office on Tuesday. (Yuichi Yamazaki/AFP/Getty Images)
The U.S. Marines said Ballard remains in Japanese custody.
His case will be handled by Japanese authorities because he was off-duty when the crime was committed and off base when he was arrested.
Japanese prosecutors will determine whether to press formal charges in the coming weeks.
If convicted, Ballard could face life in prison or the death penalty.
Interview with Sorane Sakihama produced by Nishat Chowdhury. With files from Reuters and The Associated Press.

articles.title: Israeli settlers beat press photographer as soldiers watch in West Bank
articles.summary: Jaafar Ashtiyeh was covering violence against olive farmers when settlers set upon him with the butts of their rifles Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers,…
articles.byline: William Christou in Jerusalem and agencies

blocks.text: Armed Israeli settlers beat a photographer in the presence of Israeli soldiers, hospitalising him, as he covered worsening settler violence against olive farmers in the occupied West Bank.

Jaafar Ashtiyeh, a 58-year-old veteran photographer for Agence France-Presse in Palestine, was assaulted by a group of settlers, who beat him with the butts of their rifles, despite him being marked as press. He was assaulted in view of about a dozen armed Israeli soldiers.
Ashtiyeh suffered bruises to his head and torso and was taken to hospital, according to witnesses, his family and fellow journalists.

His assault came amid a worsening wave of Israeli settler violence in the West Bank. Every year, settlers attack Palestinian farmers trying to harvest their olives – an economic lifeline for the beleaguered Palestinian economy – with few legal consequences.
This harvest season has been particularly violent as the Israeli elections approach at the end of the month.
Ashtiyeh and another AFP photographer, John Wessels, were near the northern village of Aqraba when they noticed an Israeli soldier detaining a man as local Palestinians picked olives.

A quad bike suddenly raced towards the AFP journalists on top of a hill and a man on it opened live fire, with one Palestinian dropping to the ground. He was also hospitalised, with a gunshot to the foot, according to the Palestine Red Crescent Society.

At least six other people then rushed towards the AFP journalists firing guns. As Ashtiyeh attempted to enter a car, which was clearly marked “Press”, two men jumped on him and beat him repeatedly with the butts of their rifles.
A group of at least a dozen Israeli soldiers were about 500 metres away at the time of the attack, according to Wessels.
“I could hear his screams,” said Wessels, who was also threatened at gunpoint. The assailants also took Ashtiyeh’s camera equipment.

Ashtiyeh, who is Palestinian, was conscious in a hospital in Nablus. He underwent X-rays which did not detect broken bones but he will remain in hospital for round-the-clock observation, his son, Zain Jaafar, said.
The man who initially fired the gun was wearing a long white shirt as well as military fatigue trousers and boots, which are commonly worn by soldiers, Wessels said.
AFP has asked the Israeli military for comment. Settlers are rarely arrested or charged for their attacks against Palestinians.

“We strongly condemn yet another serious attack on journalists trying to report on events in the West Bank and demand a full investigation. It is unacceptable that journalists can be beaten and robbed by armed settlers in front of Israeli security forces who made no attempt to intervene,” said Phil Chetwynd, AFP’s global news director.
The Foreign Press Association, which represents international media in Israel and the Palestinian territories, said it was “deeply alarmed”.
“Israeli authorities must investigate why soldiers present in the area did not intervene in this attack against clearly identified journalists,” it said.

“This attack is a blatant attempt to intimidate the press and obstruct accurate reporting from the West Bank. International media have a responsibility to tell all sides of the story and will not be deterred by physical assaults or threats.”
Israel was the world’s leading killer of journalists in 2025, and has killed at least 225 journalists in Lebanon and Gaza, according to the UN Human Rights Office.
Violence has flared in recent months in the West Bank with near-daily attacks, thefts or vandalism by Israeli settlers against Palestinians.
There have also been attacks against Israelis, with a Palestinian shooting dead a settler last month.
Extremist Israeli settlers have been seizing olive groves owned by Palestinians, who consider the trees a cultural symbol.
About 500,000 Israeli settlers live in the West Bank – which Israel captured in 1967 – among 3 million Palestinians. Settlements in occupied territory are illegal under international law.
Media rights groups say Israeli settlers have increasingly targeted journalists and that authorities have imposed growing impediments to coverage.

Israeli authorities have detained 19 journalists in the West Bank, including one AFP contributor, in the three years since the 7 October, 2023 Hamas-led attack on Israel, according to Paris-based Reporters Without Borders.
Agence France-Presse contributed reporting

articles.title: Fitness influencer apologizes after hitching a bike ride in the Berlin Marathon
articles.summary: The influencer, who goes by Abeeeer on popular Chinese social media platform Rednote, or Xiaohongshu, posted a "sincere apology" for violating the rules Saturday to her 520,000 followers, explaining…

image.caption: Runners compete during the 2026 BMW Berlin-Marathon on Sept. 27, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. Over 56,000 participant from 162 nations took part in the race. And one of them, a Chinese fitness influencer, was photographed riding on the back of a bike for part of it. (Maja Hitij/Getty Images)

blocks.text: World·New

The influencer, who goes by Abeeeer on popular Chinese social media platform Rednote, or Xiaohongshu, posted a "sincere apology" for violating the rules Saturday to her 520,000 followers, explaining that she was feeling physically unwell during the race but that it wasn't an excuse.
Chinese influencer Abeeeer was also dropped by her sponsor, Brooks
There's so much to love about marathon season.
The gripping accounts of elite athletes pushing themselves to the very limit. The tales of runners uplifting and supporting each other to cross the finish line. The heartache when dreams are dashed.
And then there are the people who might think, "Well, maybe no one will notice..." at a global event.
In that vein, a Chinese fitness influencer has apologized and been dropped by her sponsor after being photographed hitching a ride on a bike during the 42.2-kilometre Berlin Marathon last week.

Images of the influencer from the Sept. 27 race were first posted by the Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) Instagram account, which calls out questionable race performances. In posts from Oct. 1, the account noted that her fastest time was recorded between the 35- and 40-kilometre marks, around the time "she was spotted on the back of a bike."

A composite image of three Instagram stories posted Oct. 1 by The Official Marathon Time Integrity Unit (OMTIU) that allege to show a Chinese influencer hitching a ride in the Berlin Marathon, her times, and a finish line photo from the Sept. 27 race. (@officialunofficialtime/Instagram)
CBC News has reached out to OMTIU to ask how it obtained the photo and to the Berlin Marathon for confirmation, but has not yet received a response.

The influencer, who goes by Abeeeer on the popular Chinese social media platform Rednote, or Xiaohongshu, posted a "sincere apology" to her 520,000 followers Saturday for violating the rules. She explained that she had been feeling physically unwell during the race but acknowledged that was not an excuse.
"My behaviour to take a shortcut was disrespectful to the spirit of the marathon," she wrote in Chinese.
"I intentionally concealed this fact during my public sharing after the race. That was a truly dishonest behaviour."
The bib number shown in the images is registered to Yuanyuan Sun of China, who recorded a finishing time of 4:53:46.

items: Australian athlete apologizes for racing with diarrhea, forfeits the Beijing competition she won
Berlin Marathon winner limped to finish line after rupturing Achilles tendon chasing world mark

blocks.text: Multiple media outlets report that she had previously posted about earning a PB, or personal best, on her social media, but has since deleted her Berlin Marathon posts other than the apology.
One of her sponsors, Brooks, confirmed with CBC News that it dropped a runner after becoming "aware of the situation involving a Brooks China collaborator and the 2026 Berlin Marathon."
"After verifying the facts, Brooks China terminated its relationship with the individual," Brooks told CBC in a statement Tuesday.
"Brooks believes running should be grounded in integrity, fairness, and respect for competition."

A general view as runners compete during the 2026 BMW Berlin-Marathon on September 27, 2026 in Berlin, Germany. Over 56,000 participant from 162 nations took part in the 52nd edition of Berlin Marathon. (Maja Hitij/Getty Images)
A short history of marathon cheaters

More than 56,000 runners from 162 countries entered the 2026 Berlin Marathon. It's known for being the flattest course of the official Abbott World Marathon Majors — and therefore the fastest. About 50,000 people crossed the finish line.
And while it's not known whether anyone else attempted a shortcut this year, marathon cheating is nothing new, and what's know as course-cutting is one of the more common tactics.

items: Remembering when Rosie Ruiz stole the Boston Marathon from a Canadian
She was set to win the U.S. women's half marathon. Then a guide car made a wrong turn

blocks.text: One of the more infamous course-cutting examples is Rosie Ruiz, who was the first woman to cross the finish line of the 1980 Boston Marathon. She was crowned with a laurel wreath and didn't even seem tired.

Officials later determined that she had emerged from the crowd near the end of the race and run only about the final mile. She had qualified for Boston after taking the subway for most of the 1979 New York City marathon.
In 2011, Rob Sloan placed third in the U.K.'s gruelling Kielder Marathon. It was later revealed that he had ridden a bus for part of the course.
In 2023, Scottish ultramarathoner Joasia Zakrzewski finished third in a 50-mile race but was later disqualified for riding part of the course in a car.
The same year, the Mexico City Marathon disqualified some 11,000 runners for cutting sections of the course, including by using cars, bikes and public transit.

Natalie Stechyson has been a writer and editor at CBC News since 2021. She covers stories on social trends, families, gender, human interest, as well as general news.
